subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
that Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to propose to the House an Act to establish an independent institute which will make a major contribution to Canadian understanding and discussion of international peace and security issues. This proposed Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security should be seen in the context of increased concern in Canada over the state of East-West relations.
There have been some signs of improvement recently. However, we have not achieved an atmosphere in which conflict between East and West can be ruled impossible. The threat of nuclear war continues to loom. These spectres are of immediate concern to all Canadians. Fortunately there exists a broad-based, non-partisan consensus among us all that Canada has a right and indeed a moral obligation to play a lead role in efforts to reduce these tensions.
Canada has not stood on the sidelines. Since the Second World War, successive Canadian Governments have striven to achieve international peace and security. Highlights of this long road include Louis St. Laurent and Mike Pearson's contribution to peace-making and peace-keeping at the United Nations and Howard Green's dedication to nuclear disarmament. The valuable and timely initiative launched by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) last Autumn was another demonstration of Canada's commitment to improved East-West relations and increased global security.
In last December's Throne Speech, this Government vowed to create a publicly funded centre to gather, collate and digest the enormous volume of information now available on defence and arms control issues. Fresh ideas and new proposals, regardless of source, will be studied and promoted. That was
the statement in the Speech from the Throne. This Bill makes good the Government's commitment in that Speech from the Throne.
The purpose of the institute is two-fold. First, it will increase knowledge of issues related to international peace and security with particular emphasis on defence, arms control and disarmament. Second, it will encourage public discussions on international peace and security issues. The institute should not and could not duplicate the vast range of work already done abroad. It will develop Canadian understanding and expertise. It will bring a Canadian viewpoint and Canadian concerns to the issues of peace and security.
At present the principal sources of information on defence and arms control questions lie beyond our borders. This means that public judgment in Canada is shaped by perceptions of security devised by others and for the most part reported by others consequently. Issues of special importance to Canada have not received adequate coverage, nor have the concerns of Canadians been fully appreciated.
We cannot any longer rely in part or wholly on work done abroad. We must do more to explore these questions from a Canadian perspective. The proposed institute represents a major infusion of energy and resources by the Government of Canada. By complementing and assisting existing institutions, this independent institute will both add to the debate and increase the funds devoted to international peace and security in this country.
A prime goal will be to improve the quality and quantity of research and information available in Canada on peace and security. The institute will collect and disseminate information and ideas. The first priority will be to set up a library and data base for the voluminous published material on these questions. It will draw together and make available information. It will be a central resource for research and interest in this field by individuals as well as by groups and institutions.
The institute will promote scholarship in these areas and thus expand the pool of such talent in our country. As such, it will complement the excellent work already done, for example, in the five chairs of military and strategic studies at Canadian universities. These chairs will, of course, suffer no adverse consequences in terms of support, financial and otherwise, by the Government. The institute will have a limited inhouse research capability. It will depend largely in its early years on research by experts and institutions already existing in Canada.
The institute will not compete with existing groups, organizations and institutions. I assure the House it will not swallow

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security
up nor reduce government funding available to existing organizations. Neither is it our intention that this new institute would seek funds from non-governmental sources. It must not and it will not crowd out such worth-while bodies as the recently established Canadian Centre for Arms Control and Disarmament or overshadow the excellent work of universities from coast to coast. It will stimulate the levels of interest in peace and security to the benefit of all.
To encourage public discussion of these central issues, I expect that the institute will sponsor or hold conferences and seminars in all parts of Canada. The publication of the results of its research and activities will contribute to informed public debate in Canada. It is our intention that the institute will act as a major resource for scholars and the general public who are concerned with these issues.
The institute will be financed on an annual basis by appropriations from Parliament and will be funded equally by grants from the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence. Financing for fiscal year 1984-1985 is projected at $1.5 million, rising to $5 million by 1988-1989. The Government intends this institute to be apolitical and a centre of excellence which will serve all Canadians. It will be governed by a board of directors composed of men and women who are knowledgeable in the field and who can be relied upon to carry out their functions in a completely non-partisan manner. In this vein, myself and my colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Blais), will seek nominations from the Opposition Parties before any recommendations are made to the Governor in Council regarding appointments to the board of directors.
It is our intention that the institute will have maximum flexibility and independence. It will be free to engage in research and information gathering and dissemination as it sees fit. It will specifically be free to publish the considered findings of its researchers. It will be publicly accountable to Parliament. An annual report on its activities and finances will be submitted to Parliament through the Minister. Naturally, this report will then be referred for examination to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.
A country like Canada, which does not have nuclear weapons, depends on the persuasiveness of its ideas on defence, disarmament and arms control rather than any military leverage it has to affect these questions. The Government wants to be able to tap this new source of knowledge and ideas. It may on occasion request advice and research from the institute. In this way future governments will be able to benefit from this additional source of expert knowledge. In so doing, it will increase Canada's ability to propose realistic and imaginative solutions to the difficult and complicated questions of arms control.
The institute will be devoted to both peace and security, to defence and arms control, and disarmament. This Canadian institute will neither be exclusively devoted to strategic studies
nor to peace research. In our view, arms control and disarmament are inseparable from security.
The institute is only one manifestation of our commitment to peace and security. To encourage more public involvement in these questions we intend to increase funding for voluntary associations and private research groups. As an initial step, the Department of External Affairs disarmament fund has been increased from an original $338,000 last year to over $700,000 effective April 1. As well, funds for the study of verification procedures which are critical to successful arms control negotiations and agreements have been doubled to over $1 million.
The foundation of this institute, Mr. Speaker, is a reflection of the abiding interest of all Parties in the House and the response to many Canadians who are deeply troubled over global peace and security in the nuclear age. In planning for the institute we have sought the ideas of a wide range of Canadians and I would like to thank them for their views. This Bill has benefited from a number of constructive ideas which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) has put forward in correspondence with the Prime Minister. A number of specific changes were made which accommodate these concerns. The New Democratic Party also has put forward positive suggestions which merit serious consideration in this debate and at the committee stage. In a spirit of consensus and co-operation among all Parties, we remain open to suggestions for further change to the Bill.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that a nation's greatness lies in the power of its ideas, not only its armed might. Concern is not enough; it must be accompanied by informed views and constructive ideas. It is our hope that this institute will make a major contribution to deepening Canadian understanding of the fundamental questions of international peace and security.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be back in debate. I am pleased to be able to rise to speak on this Bill because I think there can be no question anywhere in the country that the concept of the establishment of a peace institute centred in Canada is of great importance to us. That concept enjoys wide support.
April 17, 1984

I think I owe it to the House to say at the outset that we believe the Bill that has been presented which sets up this particular institute is fatally flawed. While there have been some consultations to date with regard to improving the Bill, those consultations have not resulted in the kinds of changes that we hoped to see. We need changes that will guarantee the independence of this agency, changes that will guarantee its accountability to the House of Commons and Parliament, and changes that will ensure, more than the words of the Minister have, that there will be a complementing of the activities of agencies and institutions already engaged in the field of peace research in the country rather than a supplanting, directly or indirectly, of those agencies.
The House will know that last fall the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) asked me to undertake certain inquiries with an eye to making recommendations to him as to the policy that would be useful for a new government to follow in the field of arms control and disarmament. I have interpreted that mandate to involve public hearings across the country.
I come to this debate from five public hearings in five Canadian centres-Vancouver, Montreal, Halifax, Edmonton and Toronto-in which we had the opportunity to receive some 70 briefs from Canadian organizations and hear 92 witnesses. The most particularly valuable witnesses were those who came forward in an open session to make their contributions and to participate and express their views on an issue which they considered to be of deep concern to them. I have also had conversations with a wide range of Canadians and people outside the country regarding appropriate policies and institutions which should be established.
Without question, there is in Canada a deep and growing concern about the possibility of nuclear conflict and a deep and growing concern about whether our country is acting as effectively as it might to inch the world away from nuclear destruction. I will be reporting fully to the Leader of the Opposition later on my inquiries and recommendations. I think it might be helpful as we consider this institute if I touch on some of the testimony and bring to the House of Commons some of the views I heard in public hearings from concerned Canadians across the country, people who are not sitting in the House of Commons and are not part of the policy making, but who consider themselves very much affected by the issues that we are here discussing.
I would like to begin with a reference to testimony from a young woman who came from Great Island to the open forum at the hearing in Halifax, Nova Scotia. She came at considerable inconvenience to herself because she felt involved in these issues and wanted an opportunity to have her views expressed. She said that where she lives unemployment and poverty were very high. She said that disillusionment, apathy and despair were widespread, especially among the young, and that that disillusionment, apathy and despair were based primarily upon a deep sense of powerlessness. She suggested that many of her neighbours believed that the hearings which we were holding were simply meant to try to defuse the public's concern and
International Peace and Security
play to their undying belief in the democratic process, but that nothing would be done. That was her fear when she came. She said that she came nonetheless because she dissents from that prevailing cynicism. She believes that governments and parliamentarians will listen to people on the peace issue and will try to translate the wishes of concerned ordinary Canadians into realizable policy. She said she would go back to her community and try to convince her neighbours that it is not hopeless, that parliamentarians and governments will listen and will respond.
She spoke for herself, but she spoke for much more than herself. She spoke for a wide feeling of powerlessness, concern and a sense of being isolated in the country. As we discuss institutions today which we might establish, we, the Parliament of Canada, must be conscious that we are responding to the concerns of Canadians like the woman from Great Island and others who have nearly given up on the system and who may give up on the system if they see us put in place something that appears to be strong but in fact is not, something that appears to be independent but in fact is controlled by the Government.
One of the startling pieces of evidence that came before our hearings concerned the growth of fear among children in the country. Many of us who have children know from our own experience the extent to which they are preoccupied and concerned about these questions. My daughter, who is seven, began one or two years ago to ask me when the war is going to come, when is the world going to end? I have no recollection of putting questions of that kind when I was six or seven, nor do most of us in the House.
That is not just random observation. That expression of fear is now common in the country. Coming before our public hearings across the country were trained psychologists, some of them based at McMaster University where there is now a cross Canada study being conducted of the effect of the threat of nuclear war upon the attitudes of young people. Most of the evidence that has now been gathered is evidence that has come from the United States. It is compelling! In a study published in 1982, 3,500 American children were asked what they expected if there were to be a nuclear war. Most responded eloquently and simply by saying "I will die. We will all die". They expressed bitter resentment against adults who had already lived a full life and were putting their chance for a full life at risk.
J. C. Mack, publishing in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientist in 1981, after a survey of 1,000 schoolchildren, concluded:
-young people are growing up without the ability to form stable ideals or the sense of continuity upon which the development of stable personality structure and the formation of serviceable ideals depend.
In Vancouver we heard from the Physicians for Social Responsibility whose testimony in part I will read to the House:

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security
Scientific data indicate that a nuclear war would result in a catastrophe of degree and magnitude beyond comprehension, and that there could be no meaningful medical response to such a catastrophe. We believe that it is our responsibility, as physicians, to do all in our power to prevent what would be "the final epidemic".
There is a very real fear in the country among the sophisticated and among the innocent that we will destroy ourselves. I recognize, as does the House, that fear is no basis for foreign policy. But we recognize also that that fear is a wholly understandable reaction to a situation in which negotiations between the superpowers are broken and suspended. The number of nuclear weapons states is growing, not reducing, and the world is vulnerable to nuclear terrorists or accidents.
Canadians have cause to be afraid and, as their representatives in government and Parliament, we have a duty to address and reduce the causes of fear. I believe there is not much point in spectacular gestures. I believe we are more likely to find real progress by proceeding in a steady, sober, consistent, balanced way.
The second concern that was raised during the hearings quite consistently was a concern about how effective Canadian policy is now in responding to concerns that exist in our public and around the world. I want to summarize some of those concerns about our effectiveness that are germane to this debate.
One that was repeated frequently is that Government interest in these issues is sporadic and not well co-ordinated. That testimony is saying two things. It is making the observation that one year we have for a while a suffocation policy, then it lapses. Later we have proposals for a five-power conference, a tour and consultations, and then they lapse. But there is none of the persistence now in Canadian policy which helped former Governments achieve agreement on test bans, which helped the former Prime Minister, Mr. Pearson, contribute to the establishment of the United Nations peace-keeping operations. They are saying that there is a sporadic, inconsistent nature to our public positions on policy.
Second, there is the concern that expertise is spread around in Government. Internal expertise is not co-ordinated. Much of it is concentrated in the Department of National Defence, for example, whereas the Department of External Affairs is supposed to be the lead Department.
A second theme that was consistent is that we have a greater capacity than we are using to develop and advance specific responses to particular problems on the path to peace or on the path away from tension now. Canada is, of course, doing important work in a multitude of fields, but we are not organized to contribute up to our potential.
A third concern has to do with individual Canadians, whether they are experts or simply worried citizens, who believe that they are outside our system, that they are affected by our failures, but have no impact upon the policies we follow. They have neither the information they require nor the influence they require.
Finally, and it is very important in the context of this debate for it to be understood, there is a very real concern-the Minister made reference to it-that there is an imbalance between the emphasis on defence studies funded and encouraged by the Government, carried on across the country, and the need for studies that deal particularly with the question and with the perspective of peace, and that that imbalance has to be corrected if we are going to be as effective as the country can be in moving the world, in inching the world, away from conflict.
I think these concerns provide a useful context for the consideration of this Bill. We are not discussing here a series of policy initiatives. There was to have been a resolution presented to the House. That resolution was the subject of extensive consultation among the Parties, but that resolution has not come forward. It dealt with the general question. We are here dealing with a very specific question. We are dealing with a specific Bill to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. It is a Bill to establish one agency in a field where several agencies exist. It is a Bill that has to do with one initiative on a question where several initiatives are needed.
I make the point to the House that what we do with this institute will affect what we are able to do in other ways to increase security and world peace. If the widespread concern of Canadians over the possibility of nuclear war is addressed, if what I call the fear issue, the force of fear in the country, is addressed, that can be a means of bringing Canadians into our foreign policy debate generally.
This involvement of Canadians should not be seen, as a threat to Canadian policy. It should be seen as it is, as an unparalleled opportunity if we choose to avail ourselves of the strong, sophisticated, deep interest that exists in these questions in the Canadian public.
On the other hand, if we choose to ignore public concern in the hope that it will simply go away, we run the risk of souring the public on the ability of their elected representatives to provide leadership on this crucial issue. They will turn then, in my view, from the tone of seriousness, of sophisticated responses, a tone that marked the hearings I held, and opt for more radical or for more unilateral solutions. It is essential that we find ways to bring interested Canadians into the discussion of what their country should do in a field of policy which affects them vitally.
Of course, the issues are complex. That complexity is not only a limitation to the participation of Canadians outside Parliament; that complexity is a limitation upon the ability of Members of this House to be as informed and as effective as we should be. Elected representatives, as well as the general public, have a great need of being better informed on the technical issues relating to peace and security questions. In short, the essence of the challenge facing elected representatives is to improve the quality of knowledge upon which we might act and then enlarge, in the country and in the House, the will to act.
April 17, 1984

What is needed is an institute designed to encourage and facilitate informed debate and to produce independent, nonpartisan research and information, a world-class research and public information institution on international peace and security questions, not merely on the narrower question of arms control.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security could play a very useful role. It can make a very positive three-fold contribution to world peace and the Canadian policy: by helping the world nations to draft policies and plans likely to minimize the risk of nuclear conflict; by keeping Canada's own politicians and population well informed so as to increase their influence over public policies; finally, by symbolizing the commitment of the Canadian Government and Parliament to make the quest for peace one of our great national priorities.
Those are all worthy endeavours. In the course of this debate, we must stress the fact that the institute must have the independence, credibility and determination required to take up that challenge. In our view, this Bill does not give it the necessary independence and, therefore, restricts its credibility.
We also believe that we are duty-bound to establish clearly to what extent the activities of that organization would mesh with our national objectives to foster international peace and security. Other measures must be taken as well. The Government's internal structure must be much more coherent about any peace-related issue. The independence and integrity of research institutions already active in Canada must be maintained and protected. The Government itself must be much more open with Canadians and aware of the deep and sincere concerns about international peace.

I think it is very important, Sir, that we distinguish very clearly in this debate between the idea of an institute and the proposal that exists in this Bill. In our view it is important that there should be an independent institute centred in Canada to study peace and security. That is unquestioned; that is very clear. But we have a very deep and profound concern about this Bill, Mr. Speaker.
There have been extensive inquiries by the Government prior to this proposal being brought into the House of Commons. I rather regret that the full conclusions of those inquiries, the full range of alternatives, prepared for the Government were not presented to this Parliament. This, after all, is a parliamentary matter. We are establishing here a Canadian institute, not simply a governmental institute. It would have aided immeasurably the parliamentarians who have to make decisions on this question to have had access to the recommendations presented to the people making the inquiries by the Government and indeed to have had access to the recommendations made to the Government by those representatives.
There are, as the House will know, broadly two kinds of agencies, broadly two kinds of institutes in the world, two
International Peace and Security kinds of models, speaking generally, of approach to this question. One focuses internally. It is inward-looking. It serves the Government. It is, for example, like the National Security Council in the United States. Its purpose is to pull government advice together. Its purpose is to ensure that there is a balance in government decision-making internally to protect, for example, against an unusual influence from the military side or an unusual influence from somewhere else. It is an internal agency. That is one model which could be followed by an institute established by this Parliament. The other model is external-encouraging independent research, encouraging public information and having its focus beyond government rather than being locked into government.
Those are the two models, broadly, which exist in the world. They play very distinct roles. They are very different. However, what we have here in this institute is an attempt, in effect, to combine both approaches-not to have an agency which is strictly internal, not to have an agency which is independent and external, but to have one which combines features of both.
Our concern as we look at this Bill is that, in attempting to combine features of both, the Government creates a very real confusion about exactly what kind of agency we will have here. That confusion will almost certainly continue. That confusion, if it does continue, as I believe it will, could cripple the institute. If we are not careful in debate today, we could place upon this institute, if we adopt the Bill as it sits, restrictions which will severely, perhaps fatally, handicap its future. This institute has to be done right the first time.

I was saying that this institute has to be done right the first time because institutions define their nature in their very early days. This Bill has the following faults. First, it is confused as to what kind of institute the Government wants. Second, it is far too dependent upon government. Third, it is not accountable to Parliament. Fourth, it is not clear, despite the Minister's words, how this institute would relate to other agencies which now exist in the field.
Those are all major flaws which have to be corrected now while we are defining the nature of the institute. It would be irresponsible to let the measure proceed with these defects which could be crippling. Those of us who unfortunately have had experience in this House with offers across the floor which are not backed up in practice will require a little more than casual statements by the Prime Minister from his seat before we will be satisfied that we have an institute which guarantees the independence that is essential to this kind of undertaking.
Let me very quickly review some of the limitations upon the independence of the institute in the Bill as it now sits. I have spoken about the most dangerous of them, Clause 28, but there are also others, Clauses 6 to 8 speak about the appointment of a board of directors. Under this provision Cabinet will appoint the directors and the executive director. We have had an offer that there will be consultation with the Opposition Parties. What use is consultation when the Government makes the decision alone? This Bill gives the Government the power to make this decision by itself. There has been a proposal put forward-and the Prime Minister is interested in proposals- which would have the board of directors appointed by consensus of the standing committee of the House interested in external and defence policy. That would provide independence. That empowers the committee to appoint. It does not merely permit them to be consulted, it empowers them to appoint. That gives a much greater degree of independence than does the present measure.
Clause 14 of this Bill, which limits the kind of independent institute that we need, gives Cabinet alone the power to fix the fees of board members and fix the terms and conditions of
April 17, 1984

employment of the executive director-very powerful instruments in the hands of Cabinet. The Cabinet determines where the principal office will be. That is a fairly minor matter, but why should Cabinet decide it? Why should that not be decided by some agency more independent than the Cabinet of Canada?
In Clause 26 Cabinet has the power on its own to direct the board to make, amend or repeal any of its by-laws. In other words, what the board does after due deliberation, Cabinet can come in and has the power to undo. The effect of Cabinet coming in and undoing it is final. In effect Cabinet controls the by-laws of this institution.
I have spoken about advice to Ministers under Clause 28. Clause 29 regarding funding indicates that the institute's funding will come from "moneys apropriated by Parliament for the purpose", so it says. No other details are given, but in our view if we want to guarantee some kind of independence, consideration should be given to provisions for funding on a basis longer than one year to facilitate longer-term planning and, again, to promote the institute's independence from the Government's priorities for research.
We have had very serious and disappointing experiences with the problems of agencies that are supposed to be independent but in fact are not. There is, for example, a very clear danger in this Bill as it is written that this institute would be encumbered with political appointees who will either be reluctant to provide objective, independent analyses of, and information about, peace and security issues where such analyses would conflict with government policy or, should they be inclined to show that kind of independence, they could find themselves in the kind of situation that Doris Anderson found herself in when, as President of the Canadian Advisory Council on the Status of Women, she dared to suggest that the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as originally tabled in the House did nothing for Canadian women.
We have had too much experience with agencies that were supposed to be independent but were not independent in fact. We cannot afford to risk the independence and credibility of this institute by imposing upon it the kinds of restrictions and limitations which have so weakened institutions in other fields of policy in the country.

The Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) suggested that we should approve this Bill in principle here in the House and then work out the details in committee. What the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs called details go to the very heart of this Bill. They concern fundamental questions of independence and accountability. This Bill as it is written would allow the Government to control absolutely the work of the institute. The Government alone appoints its directors. The Government alone decides how they are paid. The Government alone has the right to dictate to the
International Peace and Security institute, to tell it what to do and then require it to do so. That is not the kind of independence which Canadians expect of this institute, nor is it the kind of independence we were led to believe this institute would have.
This Bill creates an agency which the Government can transform gradually, easily and completely into an instrument of government propaganda or indeed into an instrument of Party propaganda. If a government chose to do what this bill gives a government the power to do, the effects would spread well beyond this particular institute. This Bill effectively gives the Government the power to limit the independence of existing agencies which are working now for peace because the institute we are discussing here can move very quickly to centre stage. It will have an immediate and permanent profile high above private agencies already working in the field and it can become the standard against which they are judged.
I remind the House that this institute has behind it more than the power of example. It has the power of money. If this institute which has the power to fund other agencies or individuals is to be truly independent, no strings will be attached to that funding. But can it be truly independent when the Government alone appoints its directors, when the Government alone sets its salaries, when the Government alone can tell it what to do? That, Sir, is not independence. Without independence, this institute has the power to do more harm than good. The power this Bill gives the Government to control this institute and, by extension, to influence unduly the tone and direction of research carried out by other agencies interested in peace and security is one fatal flaw in this Bill.
Another fatal flaw in the Bill is that while this Bill gives the Government the power to control the institute, it does not give Parliament the power to hold the institute accountable. There is no accountability provision here. The Minister may lay on the Table a report. Many reports are laid on the Table of Parliament. There is no accountability of this institute to Parliament. There is instead tight and very fundamental control by the government of the day. That is inconsistent with the purposes of the Bill and is a very unfortunate aspect of it which we simply must see changed.
Reference was made to consultations that have occurred and to recommendations that have been made by the Leader of the Opposition, some of which have been adopted. Clause 5(a) of this Bill as it now reads reflects a recommendation of the Leader of the Opposition to create a national library and data base on peace and security agencies. Clause 5(e) reflects a recommendation of the Leader of the Opposition to provide facilities for conferences, seminars and funding for some other bodies.
There have been other important but minor agreements to proposals put forward by the Leader of the Opposition as a result of consultations. However, we must ask two questions about those consultations. Why did the Government agree only on the relatively minor questions and not agree on the questions which provided accountability or independence for the institute? Why did it agree only on the minor matters and disagree on the major ones?

Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) will know but apparently as the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) does not know, we in the New Democratic Party have been pursuing the subject of the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. We have been pursuing the subject of having peace research chairs to complement the chairs on strategic studies. We have been listening to the Canadian public for the last many years about their concerns with the nuclear arms race. We have participated actively in the reference in the standing committee on security and disarmament which, of course, the Right Hon. Member for Yellow-head would not know about. Therefore, it is a bit of a surprise to me to find out that the Conservative Party has just discovered the issue and the public's concern with this issue.
A Conservative Party task force held hearings in five cities and the Party discovered that the Canadian public is very concerned about the issues of international peace and security. I welcome Conservative members. I am glad they have finally discovered this.
The Minister knows that we did have an excellent series of sessions in the standing committee dealing with our reference on security and disarmament two years ago. He will also know the great importance that attaches to concerned citizens having their voices heard when it comes to such an important matter as setting up an institute for research in these subject matters. I will come back to this in a moment.
I just want to preface my remarks with not being too hasty. We agree with the Bill in principle. We agree with much of its content. I have half a dozen fairly important amendments to suggest and I will suggest them today. They will be discussed in committee. I urge the Minister and the Prime Minister, whom I am glad to see here, to ensure that the committee and its chairman, who is here as well, has time to hear the Canadian public and seriously to address amendments that would strengthen this Bill.
The Prime Minister will recall that when the International Development Research Centre was established, first reading was in the late fall of 1969. The Bill then went to the Standing Committee on External Affairs where it remained for several months. Several extremely important amendments were made. Indeed, final reading establishing the IDRC did not take place until the fall of 1970. Even the title of the centre was changed in committee. Many members on that committee took a very strong interest in the IDRC. Perhaps we cannot take that long, but I do urge that the committee not only have hearings for the members of the Canadian public who are concerned in this matter, but that it also have the careful, detailed discussion that the Bill needs when it comes to making some amendments.
There are two matters that bother me about the Bill, although it has a lot of pluses. It has not articulated in a sufficiently Canadian way the purpose of the institute. Second, Clause 28 seriously undermines the independence and the hands-off relationship that must exist between the Government and the institute.
From what the Minister said in his speech, I think he would agree that the institute must reflect the Canadian viewpoint on international issues of peace and security and start providing our own data base, information gathering, analysis and assessment. We have never had very much of this in the Government of Canada.
There must be a way, and I will not go into detail on this, in which we can make clear in Clause 4 that what we are looking for is a Canadian-based analysis and assessment of issues of
April 17, 1984

international peace and security. We are not like SIPRI, the Swedish institute, looking primarily at the whole global range of issues of international peace and security from every possible perspective.
The Minister and the Prime Minister have argued, and I agree, that we need a more Canadian perspective. In a* sense we have lost our independence in this country because we are so derivative, so dependent on the information and analysis of other countries, particularly the United States. There should be more mention in that clause of the hope that the institute will look at these matters from a Canadian perspective.
In the "purpose" clause, I would put 4(d) first, "foster, fund and conduct research on international peace and security issues of particular interest to Canadians or to the Government of Canada". That is the intention of the Government and should be the intention of all of us to emphasize.
Putting (a) first, "collect and disseminate information and ideas on international peace and security", instead of in the next section under "powers", does not give the clauses enough vigour. We hope this will be a go-getting organization doing basic and fundamental research, not just collecting information, and doing it in accordance with the needs of Canadians and from some Canadian perspective, whether it is talking about the nature of the Soviet threat or whatever. The purpose could be strengthened.
The other main area in which I have concern is Clause 28. The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead also referred to this. He suggested that it could be made more acceptable to him and his Party by changing "shall" to "may". The clause would then read:
On request therefore, the Institute may undertake research for or provide advice to the Minister in relation to any issue involving international peace and security.
I heard the Prime Minister call out that he would be quite willing to change that word from "shall" to "may". The Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead went on ranting and raving. If the Prime Minister did say that and if the Government is willing to do that, it should properly take out the clause entirely. It can remain silent. Anybody, Mr. Speaker-you, I, a citizen or group-may request the new institute to undertake something. An ordinary MP could make the request. I would hope the standing committee might do that occasionally. Anybody may request the institute to undertake research or provide advice. The institute's board would then meet and decide yes or no.
There is no reason that the clause should be in the Bill. It is not in the IDRC Act. What happens if the Government wants the IDRC to undertake something? This happened with the Conservative Government when the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was Minister. When it wanted the IDRC to do something, it had to put in a request. This was in connection with an international science and technology conference. The board met and the IDRC said: "Yes, we may do this, this and this under these conditions". This was in the 1979 period. It was perfectly all right. However, that can be done without any clause at all. I was going to
International Peace and Security
raise this point independently, that if you change "shall" to "may", you do not need the clause at all. You simply remain silent.
That is at the nub of the independence question. I do not agree with the Conservative argument; there are many other clauses in the Bill with regard to the appointment of directors by Order in Council and so on and the fact that you must have more than the tabling of the annual report and studies by the institute in Parliament and before the committee.
I judge this on the basis of similar Canadian bodies and a body like SIPRI where there are almost identical provisions. It has to report through a Minister and table its reports in Parliament. IDRC has the same arrangements, with one important exception in the choice of board of directors.
As I look back on Canadian history, I do not feel that the Government, whatever government has been in power, has abused the right to appoint directors and so on. That right may be terribly abused in appointments to the other place, but quite frankly I do not think it has in this instance. Maybe we could do as IDRC does and have a provision that two members of the board of directors may be MPs or members of the other place. That sounds terrific. I do not know whether Senator Steuart knew about this when he resigned from the IDRC after being made a senator. He could have stayed. That Act allows, as the Prime Minister will remember, up to two members of the board drawn from either House, and that might be a good idea. I feel we should explore it in committee.
What I am saying is that the other points raised by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead regarding the board, the executive director, appointments and parliamentary accountability, I believe, frankly, are adequately protected not only by this Bill but by the traditions of Canadian Governments, both Liberal and Conservative, when one talks about the Economic Council of Canada, the Science Council of Canada, the IDRC and so on. However, I do feel there is one change which might be made, and that is that after the first executive director is appointed, subsequent executive directors are chosen by the board. That is a suggestion I would make, and I have other minor suggestions in that connection.
However, it seems to me that we do not want to take away from what is the most important goal for this institute, and that is that it should freely engage in short, medium, long-term research; that it should foster such scholarly activities elsewhere, which we badly need in Canada; that it should be absolutely free to publish; and that if it is asked for advice or to do research, it may or may not do so and it may or may not do so whether the request comes from the Minister or from you or me, Mr. Speaker. That is what is particularly vital and that is why it is not even necessary to amend Clause 28. One simply removes it.
Therefore, we can liven up the purpose, make it more clearly of concern to Canadians, and in that connection, by the way, I really do not see why the Government copied the IDRC in one respect, namely, having non-Canadians on its board of direc-

tors. I believe that was and is essential for the IDRC but I do not believe it is essential for this institute. I believe this institute will be looking primarily at the Canadian perspective on international peace and security issues. In fact, if someone like George Ball or Paul Warnke or someone like that were asked to be on the board, I believe it would be of some embarrassment to them. The institute can always get their advice and, indeed, I am sure it would, as we all do. However, I am not at all sure that that particular copying of the IDRC legislation was necessary or desirable.
I will have specific clauses to help strengthen the purpose section. In the powers section we would put the collecting and disseminating of information. In connection with the publishing of studies, I would draw the attention of the Minister to Clause 5(c). This is kind of a mixed up clause. It states that the institute may:
-publish studies and reports prepared for the use of the institute and publish or otherwise disseminate scientific, technical or other information as it sees fit;-
The words "scientific, technical" came from the IDRC. I would say that that clause should simply read that the institute may "publish or otherwise disseminate reports, studies or other information relevant to its purpose". That is nice, clean wording. The phrase "for the use of the institute" is not, I believe, what the Government intends.
There are three kinds of studies and reports which the institute might undertake. It might do inhouse research. It will have a small inhouse research capacity. It might contract out research for its use. However, there might be research done out there-and the Minister pointed out how anxious he would be that this would complement rather than supplant research and scholarly activity-and the institute might well pick up a piece of research done out there, think it extremely valuable to its purpose and agree to publish it, even though it was not for its use, if the outside person wanted it published. Therefore, I simply guard against the use of the words "for the use of the institute". In fact, I would remove them entirely, and have clause 5(c), a very important clause, simply read" publish or otherwise disseminate reports, studies or other information relevant to its purpose".
While I am on Clause 5,1 have another small point I would like to make. In order to ensure that the institute itself is not going to seek funds in the private sector, it would be quite simple to change Clause 5(g) from "acquire any property, money or securities by gift" to "accept any property". That is a more benign phrase, and I will be putting forth that amendment in committee. I am just giving the Minister lots of notice on these amendments.
Clause 7 reads:
The Executive Director shall be appointed by the Governor in Council to hold office for a term not exceeding five years.
Any executive director, subsequent to the first director who would be appointed in this way, should, I feel, be appointed on the recommendation of the board of directors.
With respect to Clause 18, I have already mentioned the question of non-Canadians on the board and I would appreciate a response to that at some time. As I said, I believe that is entirely appropriate for IDRC. It is certainly entirely appropriate for SIPRI. By the way, SIPRI responds to a Minister, the Minister lays its reports before Parliament and SIPRI is extremely independent. So we should take another look at Clause 18.
I have already discussed at length why Clause 28 should be removed. I agree with all other speakers, including the Minister himself, that one of the most important things is that the institute should have an arm's length relationship with the Government, and that it should be genuinely able to decide for itself on the research it does and the advice it gives.
On the financial side, the Minister mentioned that the funding would be $1.5 million in the present year, rising to $5 million by 1988-1989-it could well rise more than that, I assume-and that it would be jointly funded by annual grants from the two Departments, the Department of National Defence and the Department of External Affairs.
Again, going back into history, if I may, to IDRC-and the reason I compare it so much with IDRC is that it is so similarly structured-as I remember, IDRC was initially funded from an appropriation by CIDA, but it very soon achieved its own separate line item. I would hope that the same would be the case here. Frankly, I believe it should start immediately with its own separate line item, and I will have an amendment to that effect when we come to committee.
In summary, this Party has been in favour, is in favour, and shall continue to be in favour of such an institute being established, a Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. We believe it is badly needed. Far from suffocating other bodies engaged in this goal, we feel it will encourage them, help fund them, and will produce a good deal more scholarly material. I believe, frankly, it is superior to the Australian institute, which I received information about yesterday, which is tied solely to the Australian national university. I believe, if the purpose is made clearer, that this institute will for the first time-and perhaps this is something which governments should have done long since-provide a scholarly Canadian assessment from a Canadian perspective as well as from a world perspective on the issues of international peace and security.
I like the emphasis, as we all do, on peace and security issues. Of course, as the Minister has said, this will include strategic studies, although we have more accomplished in that field already. We want the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to have time. That is what worries me more than anything else.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am very pleased to speak today on second reading of this Bill to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, particularly after listening to the arguments of our two Opposition colleagues. I know full well that the former Leader of the Opposition had spoken at length on the question of independence, and particularly on the appointment of members of the new institute's board of directors dealt with in Clauses 6 to 8.
As I was listening to his remarks and his suggestion about Committee members reaching a consensus and making recommendations concerning appointees to the institute, I could just see him and the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) being on the same Committee, and I was wondering how we
International Peace and Security might possibly reach a consensus if those two sit on the same Committee.
Mr. Speaker, I do think we would be expecting too much if we thought that the Committee might agree on 27 appointments. Should the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) have a precedent in mind, perhaps he would enlighten us before the Bill is referred to Committee for consideration. I noticed that he and our colleague of the NDP did not see any need to dwell upon the first few clauses of the Bill dealing with the purpose and powers of the institute.
Therefore, we can safely assume that the two Opposition Parties see nothing wrong with the principle of the Bill and that their complaints bear on minor details. As I said earlier, the matter of appointments did come up-I can still recall the position taken by the Hon. Member for York-Peel during the Committee study on Latin America. Once again, how could he go along with a consensus on appointments? History usually repeats itself, Mr. Speaker, and that explains why I feel that such a solution is unrealistic.
Besides, our colleagues opposite always talk about the responsibilities of the Government concerning foreign corporations. In that respect, I think that the Government should indeed take its responsibilities. Given the impartial nature of the activities of the institute, the Prime Minister gave the Leader of the Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party the assurance that they would be consulted about the appointments. I do not see what more can be said at this stage but, in the course of Committee proceedings, we might come up with alternative solutions which would be more practical than the one advocated by the Member for Yellowhead.
With respect to Section 28,1 think that many Members are concerned about the fact that the Minister can ask the Institute to give him advice or to undertake research work. Mr. Speaker, considering that public funds will have been allocated to an institute, whenever the Minister needs some advice to develop policies, the best source of information will certainly be this institute. The latter will certainly be in a position to provide him with ideas, not necessarily ideas that will please him, but well informed advice. Everyone in this House will recognize the need to establish an agency which will make a regular, in fact an ongoing examination of issues as important as international peace and security. I do not know to what extent the Minister may be criticized for asking the advice of this institute. Should this agency be established only to be ignored, either by the Government, by the Members of the Committee or by the public? I believe that the Minister should have the privilege of using the valid advice of the Institute in developing his policies, and, for this reason, I have no difficulty in accepting that the Minister should be allowed to ask for the advice of the Institute, even though, in fact, he does not necessarily have to follow such advice. The Institute will strictly be a major source of information for him. Since the

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security Canadian public will be paying for the Institute, I think that it would be . .. Would it be better were the Institute to refuse to provide advice to the Minister, who would then have to spend additional public funds to have the same research done elsewhere? I wonder to what extent this can be considered as limiting the independence of the Institute since the contents of the advice given will not be dictated by the Minister. In this regard, I believe that the Minister should in fact be able to avail himself of the good judgment of the Institute and I have no difficulty in accepting that.
As far as salaries and benefits are concerned, I know that they do worry the Hon. Member for Yellowhead. Are we going to ask the Committee to set this gentleman's or that lady's salary, to approve the Institute members' expense account? The Hon. Member for Yellowhead said that he did not want the Government or the Cabinet to set either the salaries or the expense accounts. Who will do it then, Mr. Speaker? Should we ask, for instance, the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to determine how much money this or that person will be paid, as he suggested initially? I believe that, first, this would be asking the Committee to get stuck in red tape, and second, that it would be quite irresponsible for the Government to delegate this administrative responsibility to people other than those who, finally, are accountable to the public for it.
Section 26, which also seems to worry our friends of the Official Opposition, concerns the by-laws which will be passed by the Institute. The responsibility always comes back to the Government in the end, but, in any case, I believe that this type of provision is quite common and has already been applied to nearly all the Crown Corporations established to this date.
As we all know, this is not done regularly or routinely. It is the kind of unusual action which must be warranted and which in any case has not been the current practice these last few years, namely that the Government should issue Orders in Council which go against the by-laws of its own corporations, institutes or agencies.
I therefore do not share the concern of our friends opposite about the methods or the relationship between the Government and the Institute. I believe that the Canadian public feels the need for a group specializing in these matters which affect all of us. The Canadian public needs more information, and we do expect to obtain data of a less complex nature than those which come to us from all kinds of sources, especially foreign sources. This is one of the purposes of the Institute. Everyone is concerned by this issue. There are bonafide groups from all across the country which certainly want to have access to such an agency. In particular, I know hundreds of students who are concerned by the issue of international peace and who will certainly want to use the data, the library facilities and all the information compiled by the Institute.
In such wide-ranging negotiations, Mr. Speaker, the way a country is knowledgeable and familiar with the issue at hand probably weighs more heavily than the sheer number of its population or its political views. It is in that sense that, in my opinion, with such an institute, Canada will play a much more significant role than we would expect in terms of its current political, demographic or economic power. If our politicians on both sides of the House really know the issue inside out and can count on applied research done by experts totally dedicated to this cause, we as a country will certainly have greater influence on the international scene and more input in drafting our own defence and peace policies.
A lot of energy is being spent right across the country in the quest for peace-we know that some people are deeply committed to that endeavour-and the various groups will finally discover the kind of outlet they need-not within but close to the Government-to exchange ideas, air their views and propose their own solutions. Those discussions will certainly be launched from coast to coast and be of great use to all those who have public responsibilities. In that sense, I am glad to see that our colleagues opposite are generally favourable to the establishment of the institute. Once in Committee, they will have every opportunity to debate at length the various aspects that bother them, but I would hope that they will not tie up the proceedings by arguing about insignificant details. I know that our NDP colleague intends to introduce a series of amendments. Since the institute will not be the exclusive realm of the Government, because the main issue is much more important that any political faction, I am convinced that the proposed amendments will be given due consideration.
On the other hand, we should not attempt to come up with an organization so far removed from reality that we would defeat our own purpose. I heard the Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) insisting that the institute must be independent and, in the same breath, urging that it be consistent with our national goals. How can he reconcile that? That is what he said, and the blues are there to prove it, but I can see that it is not going to be easy. They also said that the institute must be accountable. Well, Mr. Speaker, that should not cause any problem since an annual report will be tabled in the House and, as we all know, such reports can indeed be taken under consideration since they are automatically deemed to be referred to the appropriate Committee. In other words, the members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence will have all the time in the world to scrutinize the reports of the institute.
This is a new procedure, of course, so perhaps it slipped the mind of our colleague from Yellowhead, although he is usually aware of the intricacies of our Standing Orders. As a matter of fact, if he were to sit on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, he would certainly be in a position to read the annual reports and insist that they be gone over with a fine comb during Committee proceedings.

I have no qualms about the financial accountability of the institute. For instance, he spoke about two models-an instrument of internal information and an instrument of external information-and said that those were the only possibilities, yet he concluded that we are trying to have a little bit of both. In fact, Mr. Speaker, if we can at last establish a direct link between the people who are genuinely interested in this cause and who often are experts-some of them may be self-appointed experts-and the institute first, then with Parliament and the Government which will certainly act upon the recommendations of the institute, I think, Mr. Speaker, that that would complete the full circle. I am therefore convinced that, by operating along the lines proposed in this Bill, the Institute will certainly influence Government policy and the views of the Opposition, and this will be important. The Institute will be at the nerve center of all the activities related to the quest for peace and disarmament and actually everybody will benefit from it. As for the groups, and I know that the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead has probably met with hundreds of them which are concerned with disarmament, they always feel somewhat at a loss when they have to gain access to the system. I for one, I believe that the Institute can certainly be a window opening on the system with a capital "s" since some of these groups now deal with the Department of National Defence while others call on the Department of External Affairs without really knowing who is mainly responsible for such matters in the system. In this regard, the Institute will certainly be an access to the system for all these groups and individuals.
These groups will also certainly be useful to the Institute. I am certain of it. The Bill mentions the possibility of having research work farmed out or of using the results of research carried out by others, and there are about fifteen groups in Canada which are particularly interested in research in this field. The Institute can certainly use them. Finally, the Institute will be able to work in co-operation instead of always looking for confrontation.
The Members opposite claim to be against confrontation, but, to this date, I believe that in the quest for peace, there often is a high degree of confrontation. We know that there is a communications gap, especially where the pacifist groups are concerned, even though they often pursue the same objectives as we all do. The fact that the Institute will distribute information, develop ideas and communicate with these people will certainly bring about the new consensus we all need. I believe that our energies must be gathered together, and the focus of this concentration will certainly be the new Institute.
Mr. Speaker, I am more than happy to see that the commitment voiced in the Speech from the Throne is on the point of becoming a fact and that we are finally going to be able to pass this Bill with the co-operation of our friends opposite within the next few weeks. I am convinced that, in committee, with the suggestions put forward by both sides of the House,
International Peace and Security we shall be able to finalize the text of the Bill to make it as acceptable as possible to all without taking anything away from the very concept of the Institute. We already agree on what the purpose and the powers of the Institute should be. All that remains to do is therefore to work out the administrative details.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that the House is dealing today with a subject which will certainly interest today's generation, as well as all future generations. In fact, the closer we come together, the greater the degree of confrontation there is and the more we look for some way to break the deadlock. This Bill represents a commendable effort on the part of the Government, and with the support of the other political parties, we can all do our share and contribute to the debate. I am convinced that the originality of the studies and the Canadian-ization of solutions will contribute to the international exchange of views. subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-32 is an extremely important and timely Bill. It is timely because of the widespread and growing fear and concern that is felt and expressed by thousands of ordinary Canadians that not enough is being done to move the hands of the nuclear clock back from midnight. It is also important because that fear and concern is justified.
Less than ten years ago I had the privilege of being part of an annual Remembrance Day service when it was possible to say with hope and gratitude that, for the first time since World War II, no wars were being fought anywhere in our world. Although the world was not calm, at least it was, for once, at peace.
Today, less than ten years later, the world is at war in far too many places. Tension, military confrontation and the concomitant risk of resort to the use of nuclear arms are greater threats than any of us can possibly believe we can afford.
The Bill is important because an institute for peace and security could contribute greatly if its mandate is designed properly. Imagine the progress toward true peace that effective research into conflict resolution and verification procedures alone could have. Canada is especially poised in the world as it sits today. We are one of the very few nations left with sufficient credibility around the world to produce such research and have it seen to be objective and intended purely for the development of international peace and harmony.
As Members of the House know too well, credibility is much harder to obtain than it is to lose. It is precisely because of that credibility that we have two obligations. The first is an obligation as a nation to do all that we can. An institute with a proper mandate is an important part of that goal. It is for that reason that we on this side believe that a Canadian institute
April 17, 1984

designed to research ways to make peace happen should be created.
The second obligation arising from that first obligation is to make sure that as we debate this Bill and create this institute we are doing the right thing. It is to make sure that we are creating an institute that, by the very nature and words of its creation, can have credibility. That is why the issue that will be raised by our side consistently throughout this debate will be the question of the quality of the independence of this institute.
Let me divert and talk about the process of arriving at non-partisan agreements. Since coming to the House I have been privileged on two occasions to witness Parties in the House being able to resolve issues or resolve their own conflicts. One such case was referred to by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) when he talked about the way at least two Parties in the House were able to come to some agreement on the potential of a peace resolution. The other involved a decision by the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox) to allow the question of broadcast strategy to be referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture prior to the adoption of a firm position by the Government. I believe he did so because some of us told him that the Committee could do good work if it were given a chance. This, the Committee did. It adopted a unanimous report. Much of that report has shown up in the Minister's broadcast strategy.
I find it offensive that the opening comments of the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre) contained an assumption in advance of any debate in the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence that consensus is not possible. If that is the attitude, Mr. Speaker, that will be carried into the Committee, then, of course, consensus is not possible because it is that attitude which makes consensus impossible.
I want to put all my comments on the question of independence and the quality of research that needs to be done in the context that I believe consensus is possible. I believe consensus on this issue, among others, and perhaps on this issue above all others, is preferable to conflict. I suppose that is one of the reasons the process which led to the introduction of this resolution and the termination of a conversation between the offices of the Leader of the Government and the Leader of our Party concerns us, and why that conversation terminated so quickly. It should be clear to Members of the Government that an agreement worked out which would have overcome what is sometimes a natural tendency to mistrust each other would have been infinitely preferable.
Let me come to the Bill briefly, Mr. Speaker. Let me say a couple of words about what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) had to say. I think what is instructive in his speech is that within five seconds of opening his speech today he thought it was important to refer to the creation of "this independent institute". It was his opening phrase and he returned to that phrase at least three times to
International Peace and Security
my knowledge; the blues may show more. One cannot be surprised, therefore, as we read the Bill that has been tabled in the House and we know the question of independence is apparently important in the language of the Minister and that the question of the quality of the independence was part of the discussion between the Leaders' offices, if we ask where are the changes from the draft Bill to this Bill to guarantee that independence? They are not here.
The Minister indicated that the primary purposes of this Bill were, in his words, to increase knowledge of issues and to encourage public discussion. Both of those are positions we support. Both of those are terribly important these days. But, Sir, if the purpose of the institute is to do those things, then how can it be reasonable to argue that the institute should have an obligation to conduct research for the Minister at the Minister's suggestion? The Hon. Member for New Westmin-ster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) in her comments indicated that perhaps the answer was to abolish Clause 28. That may well be. But it must be clear to the Minister that we believe the Government should understand very early in this debate that it may ask this institute on behalf of Canadians to be one of two things, not both of two things. It can ask this institute to conduct research, to do issue-based research, to make comments to help Canadians and others perhaps understand these issues, or it can perform as a research arm of the Minister advising the Minister. But it cannot, with credibility, do both.
If the Secretary of State for External Affairs looks a little perplexed when I make this point, then let me take him back, through you, Sir, to a debate that occurred, again in the broadcast and communications committee, about two years ago on a similar kind of matter when the Government brought in its estimates of funding for the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council and, for presumably good reason, announced it was prepared to permit an increase in the funding of that Council provided that that agency began to do research into specific areas that the Government wanted researched. If the Minister wants to check, he will find that the hue and cry and furore that created in the academic community was unequalled in the five years previous, because the perception was created that the Government proposed to use an independent research agency to do the work the Government wanted done, not the work which the research community believed needed to be done.
We have exactly the same question here, Mr. Speaker. It is not going to go away. The quality of the credibility for all of us-for all the folks in the world-of the research that comes out of this institute will depend upon the degree to which it is perceived to be free from the possibility of direction from the cabinet and government of the day.
Let me go back for a moment to an example, if I may, Sir. In this world the greatest issue confronting us is to find a way to reduce tension. The way, in my view, to do that is to do everything we can in the area of conflict resolution. The quality of the work done on conflict resolution, if it is perceived as being dependent upon the Government or if it is perceived as being directed through Government policy, will

International Peace and Security suffer. It must be independent and be seen to be independent. Let us make that point over and over until it is adopted. Alone in the area of reasearch, if I may stay with it, I think there is a legitimate concern as to the degree to which this institute, for the best possible reasons, may impact upon other research agencies in the areas of defence, arms control and strategic studies.
It will be very important in committee, I say to the Minister, that the words he used which are different from the Bill, namely that this institute will have "limited inhouse research capability", be clarified. I may say to Members of the House-I say this with a sense of humour for the moment, not in a partisan way-that we are getting used to Liberals clarifying their comments. But I say seriously to the Minister that this issue of the degree to which this agency will complement and be guaranteed to complement in research terms is an issue. Some people outside as well as some people in this House have a fear that some other Minister, at some other time, will talk about the funds in this agency as meeting the Government's commitment to increased research as opposed to what we believe it should be-an independent, important and special project delivered with public funding through this institute. I never want to see anybody being able to turn to the research community of Canada and say: "We haven't really reduced funds for research in this country because look at the total, including this". That is a concern I have personally, Mr. Speaker.
While I am on that point and just before breaking for lunch, the Minister ought to know that in a way he has in fact introduced a note of confusion today. I may say it is a shame that Members of the Liberal back-bench chose to stop the practice of asking questions of the Minister today because that might have helped the whole debate. But the question will be asked of the Minister, if this agency is to do the work it is supposed to do, why does he talk about separate funding, doubling, for apparently separate work and verification procedures? subtopic: FINANCE
FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the results of a recent study by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business confirm that excessive taxation by all levels of government is driving businesses and jobs out of Canada.
Almost half the 300 smaller Ontario manufacturing firms contacted responded to the survey. Of those 16 per cent already have a plant or branch in the United States and a quarter of them have investigated such a move. John Bulloch warns that 75,000 manufacturing jobs are at risk in Ontario alone.
The businesses contacted believe that Canadian labour costs are at least 10 per cent higher than those in the U.S. They know that the cost of meeting labour standards is higher here and that municipal, business and payroll taxes greatly exceed those in the U.S. Excessive government regulation at all levels is at the top of the list. All levels of government share responsibility for taking the action required to keep businesses in Canada.
The federal Government has the responsibility to take the lead by reducing the onerous burden of payroll taxes and by seeking the co-operation of all levels of government to stop this drain of jobs into the United States.

subtopic: POTATO INSPECTION SERVICES IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
POTATO INSPECTION SERVICES IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I would like to discuss an issue of utmost importance to the potato industry on Prince Edward Island concerning the inspection of potatoes. Potatoes exported from P.E.I. have achieved a standard of high quality throughout the world. It is this reputation which has made the potato industry so important to P.E.I. Good inspection practices for potatoes are essential to keep this reputation. Unfortunately the P.E.I. potato industry has been on a backslide due to the decline in the quality of these inspection services.
The reason for this has been the program of cross-utilization of inspectors which has been used over the past few years. Cross-utilization of inspectors, the use of table stock inspectors to inspect seed potatoes and vice versa, does not work. This is leading to disaster within the industry, as potatoes are being placed on the market which will damage P.E.I.'s reputation for high quality.
There is a continuing downgrading of inspection services on P.E.I. which is placing the industry in jeopardy. Not only has cross-utilization of inspectors hurt the industry, but the federal Government has indicated that it may be cutting back further on mandatory potato inspection. One government official has stated that the reason for further cutbacks in inspection services is due to the lack of available funds. I find this explanation totally unacceptable. The federal Government can find money for countless, less worth-while projects which are not nearly as important to the economy. The Prince Edward Island Potato Producers' Association has pointed out that the honour system does not work, that we need only look to Maine as an example of this, and that should these cutbacks occur we will certainly lose our world renowned status. I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to study this serious situation surrounding inspection practices.
