subtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PEACE TAX
CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PEACE TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, two years ago the Queen proclaimed our new Constitution along with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This guarantees to all Canadians freedom of conscience and religion. Canada has long recognized freedom of conscience as a valid reason for refusing to serve in the military. In the two world wars many conscientious objectors found alternate ways of serving their country.
Today many Canadians are concerned about the spiralling arms race and Canada's part in it. They object to paying taxes for this insanity which threatens our world with nuclear holocaust. People who object to supporting the arms race with their taxes want a positive alternative which will neither do violence to their conscience nor destroy their reputation as good citizens.
I call upon the Government to establish a peace tax fund which could be used for such items as peace research and promoting international understanding. People who contributed would receive a 100 per cent income tax credit up to the percentage of their tax normally allocated to defence spending.

April 17, 1984
A peace tax fund would not only make freedom of conscience a reality, it would also make a positive contribution to Canadian security and world peace.

subtopic: EFFECT OF CUSTOMS SEARCH PROCEDURES ON INDUSTRY
EFFECT OF CUSTOMS SEARCH PROCEDURES ON INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canadian tourism is suffering at the hands of Canada Customs border officials. I have received correspondence from as far away as Florida where newspaper articles have slammed Canada Customs in no uncertain terms.
The St. Petersburg Times quoted Barry Pitegoff, Director of Research for the Florida Division of Tourism, who was harassed at the border. Ironically, he was heading to Charlottetown to present an address on hospitality at the annual meeting of the Tourism Industry Association of Canada.
In another instance, country music singers Shelly West and David Frizell have vowed never to return to Canada to perform. They were subjected to a strip search at a border crossing at Windsor, and were left embarrassed and devoid of personal dignity. Press coverage of this nature in the United States is doing untold harm to the Canadian tourism industry as a whole.
Reports claim that female customs officials tend to be the most severe with travellers. I am aware that the constant search for illegal goods must take place, but the situation is out of control. I would ask the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith) to speak with his colleagues at Canada Customs on this pressing and urgent matter. The present situation is counter-productive to reversing the sky-rocketing tourist deficit.

subtopic: NON-ENFORCEMENT OF FAMILY MAINTENANCE ORDERS
NON-ENFORCEMENT OF FAMILY MAINTENANCE ORDERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to bring to the attention of the House a case which dramatically illustrates the serious inadequacies of the present system for enforcing support and maintenance orders.
Ms. Kerry Moore, who resides in Brandon, Manitoba, is owed more than $5,000 in maintenance payments by her ex-husband, money she has been unable to collect despite numerous legal proceedings which began in January, 1982. Meanwhile she struggles to support herself and her daughter. Her husband has failed to appear in court on more than one occasion, he has ignored court orders to make payments on his arrears, and at present his whereabouts are unknown.
Divorce is difficult enough without the added complications which result when one spouse does not meet his or her
maintenance obligations. All too often women are the victims of this system and many of them, because of their Financial circumstances, find it very difficult to pursue legal action. I regret that some have simply given up.
The Government has, at long last, indicated its willingness to establish a central registry which would keep track of all maintenance and support orders. That would be a good start. But as Kerry Moore's case demonstrates, it is not enough. Along with it must go the power to enforce the orders. Otherwise, single parents like Kerry Moore will continue to be caught between courts which tell them they have legal rights, and a system which offers them little means to protect those rights.

subtopic: CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT PRIORITIES
CONDEMNATION OF GOVERNMENT PRIORITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with priorities. During the last year western grain producers have been given a good indication of how low their priority really is with the Government. First the grain freight rates were raised by 20 per cent on January 1, and we can expect a raise of another 300 per cent in the next couple of years. Meanwhile the railways are guaranteed a 40 per cent profit on the movement of grain.
Branch lines are being abandoned, and each abandoned line increases farmer costs and decreases railway costs. Taxes on petroleum have pushed the cost of farm fuel and fertilizers up by 300 per cent or more. Meanwhile the oil companies are given billions of dollars in incentives and tax concessions.
Farm Credit Corporation interest rates have been increased to 14 per cent and 16 per cent. Meanwhile banks are increasing profits because the inflation and the real interest rate spread. Initial grain prices have been lowered.
The Government is unwilling to take a chance on farmers, while it risks billions of dollars on Massey-Ferguson, Chrysler, and other large corporations. Western grain stabilization money which could help many farmers survive sits idle while the Cabinet twiddles its collective thumbs. All these facts, Mr. Speaker, indicate that the Government's priorities are far from the prairie farm.

subtopic: DENIAL OF ELIGIBILITY TO FORMER OVERSEAS VOLUNTARY
DENIAL OF ELIGIBILITY TO FORMER OVERSEAS VOLUNTARY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of my constituents is a married civil engineer who selflessly undertook voluntary work overseas for a period of time which proved to be over a year. He received no remuneration for this work other than food and lodging. Upon returning to Canada and being unable to find work, this man learned that he was
April 17, 1984

ineligible for unemployment insurance benefits even though he had accumulated many times the number of sufficient insurable weeks prior to his departure overseas.
Section 18 of the Unemployment Insurance Act stipulates that an extension to the 52-week qualifying period of 20 insurable weeks within the 52-week period prior to a benefit claim may be granted if the claimant proves to the Unemployment Insurance Commission that he or she was not employed in insurable employment during that time because he or she was incapable of working due to a prescribed illness, quarantine, or pregnancy, was in jail, was in attendance at a prescribed course of instruction, or was in receipt of temporary worker's compensation benefits. The qualifying period would thus be extended by the number of weeks a person was in jail, ill, or so forth.
I am suggesting that we treat this formerly employed Canadian at least as well as we treat criminals. The same fate awaits graduate students who study abroad for over a year, or teachers and professionals who are on extended sabbaticals. Is it just to extend the qualifying period for criminals, persons who already place a great strain on our national economy, and do nothing for individuals such as my constituent who contribute to our national and international well-being by volunteering their expertise in countries less fortunate than ours?

subtopic: PLIGHT OF SINGLE WOMEN PENSIONERS

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance. It concerns some very serious changes that are taking place in the managerial level of the Bank of Montreal. Yesterday we learned that the Government has given approval for upwards of 50, 60, and perhaps more positions in that Canadian bank to be taken over by American citizens, including the chairman of the bank, who is an American citizen and who recently said of the Bank of Montreal: "The bank is no longer a Canadian bank with international appendages. It is an international bank that happens to be based in Canada." Is the Minister concerned that this Americanization of key positions in that bank will lead to banking decisions being made in Canada that are not in the national interest of Canada?

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING
subsubtopic: BANK OF MONTREAL-CHANGES IN EXECUTIVE POSITIONS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. I will give a little explanation. The Bank of Montreal has indeed become a very important international institution. In that sense I certainly welcome the fact that Canadian financial institutions are going to be able to take on other institutions on a world-wide scale. This country can afford large institutions that are able to compete around the world.
As to knowing whether decisions would be made contrary to the national interest, I remind my colleague that banks in Canada are very heavily regulated. They are supervised by the Superintendent of Banks. Also, they are in constant contact with the Bank of Canada.
As far as management in that institution is concerned, at the present time there are 196 officers in Canada with the rank of vice-president or higher. Out of that number, 19 are non-Canadians, including 12 Americans. In posts abroad, there are 15 Canadians in senior positions. I am not nervous about there being 19 foreigners working for the Bank of Montreal in Canada. There are 15 Canadians working abroad for that bank, in senior positions. This is 19 out of 196 positions. We should let those institutions try to recruit the best people for the job, realizing that there are people in Canada for those jobs, as 90 per cent are now Canadian citizens.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that Bill C-32, an Act to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning we had laid before the House our general support for an institute of this nature. We had indicated our reservations about the independence which this Bill appears not to grant to the institute proposed. I had come in my remarks to some concerns about research in general.
It seems appropriate, therefore, to refer Members of the House to an article in today's Toronto Star written by Mr. Adam Bromke of McMaster University. The very concern about this institute's relationship to research organizations is raised and very clearly expressed.
I left off referring to what I think is a confusion caused by the remarks of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and I would like to return to that briefly. The Throne Speech talked about the need for an organization to digest, disseminate and collate information. It had a second paragraph which talked about the Government's intention to increase its funding for voluntary associations and private groups. I think most members of the community read those two paragraphs as one, as part of the same organization.
I was confused, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure I am not alone, in fact I know I am not alone in my confusion, when the Minister in his comments earlier today referred to the Government's intention to proceed whith this Bill as it stands and, at the same time, increase funding for private organizations and double separate research funds for verification procedures. Clearly at some point the Government will have to answer the question as to what the relationship is between the institute and its research activities and private sector organizations.
I want to put on the record something that is of personal concern. I would hope that this institute will honour as completely as possible the words the Minister actually used even though the Bill does not use the words. The Minister said that this institute should have a limited inhouse research capacity. It is my personal view, and I hope we will be able to deal with this in committee when we get there, that it is important in terms of this institute's relationship with the universities and with the other research institutions of Canada that to the greatest extent possible this organization be a funder of research in Canada more than a doer of research. I think that is essential if the other research institutions are to believe that this institute is not in fact a competitor and a threat. I am
International Peace and Security confused by the Government's words in the Minister's speech.
I make that point because I think it is essential that it be clarified.
Finally, in the couple of minutes I have left, I want to deal with a few points made by the Hon. Member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett). She raised what I think is a most interesting point with regard to the apparent similarity of the appointments to the board of this proposed institute and those of the IDRC. The point she was making, I take it, was that while there may be some justification in the other operation for non-Canadian appointment, there may not be, in her view, that justification here. That is a point which had not occurred or been brought to me before. I think it is important.
I think we will have to be very careful on that point in committee.
I was confused by the Hon. Member's comment that she was not worried about the total control of appointments to the board by the cabinet of the day, given her apparent willingness to allow the cabinet of the day to make those appointments. I think it is essential in understanding all of the concerns which the research community has, that we have and several of the organizations deeply interested in peace have, that if one is to understand the importance of independence, Mr. Speaker, then one has to deal directly with the degree of potential control, not just the degree of actual control that is available to the cabinet of the day with regard to this proposed institute.
I want to stress to the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam and to all Members of the House that here nonpartisanship is of the essence. It is absolute in dealing with peace matters. I want to put right back on the record that I think the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam should rethink that concern.
It would be extremely useful if we could come to an agreement across the floor of the House to allow some body other than the Cabinet to have a deep and serious say, and preferably control on a consensus basis, regarding the appointments that are made to the board. I think that if Members were to understand the potential value of having the external affairs committee make those appointments on a consensus basis, it would be invaluable both for the institute in appearing to be independent, and invaluable for all of us in being able to say it is independent. If we can come to an understanding of that, at least we will have gone a long way toward taking what we all believe in its conceptual framework is an important and useful idea and making it what it really ought to be-an organization as non-partisan as possible to be of use in what I think we all believe is extremely important, the search through whatever means possible for an everlasting peace.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I will try to answer it in two parts. One is the concern we have about the proposed method of appointment, and then I will try to answer directly his question about what we believe would be better.
There is always a concern in terms of the Cabinet when by Order in Council appointments may be seen to be or may in fact be not as non-partisan as they should be. I think the Member would understand that. I think we are somewhat reluctant to accept the simple statement that the Leader of the other Opposition Party and the Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition will be "consulted" as to whether that is good enough. On this issue we do not believe it is. What we believe ought to be done and what we should look for is a method whereby the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence could be asked to make appointments to the board on the understanding that the Committee had to operate on a consensus basis and not on a simple majority vote basis. We believe that out of the process of coming to agreement would come non-partisan appointments.
That is the process we believe should be used to make these appointments. The Hon. Member may ask whether Parliament could do that. I know of no mechanism that allows Parliament to do that as a whole. That is why I think we believe the committee should have that power.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in this House the Conservative Party is on record as voting in favour of testing of the Cruise missile. The Conservative Party is on record as supporting the construction of components for nuclear weapons delivery systems. The external affairs critic and a number of other caucus members have publicly endorsed the position of the United States in Central America. Could the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley) explain the contradiction of how the Conservative Party can in fact be supporting peace and disarmament on the one hand, while in fact in this House and on the public record it is supporting and endorsing activities which certainaly are not, in the minds of most Canadians, conducive to this nation's movement toward peace and disarmament? Could the representative from the Tory Party explain that contradiction?

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are also on record as supporting NATO. I presume the Hon. Member would go further in his comment and suggest, as he has argued before, that support of NATO is in conflict with the view we in this Party share which supports peace and disarmament. If the Hon. Member finds that there is confusion, I believe it is in his mind.
The issue for us, and I hope for the Hon. Member, is that whatever one's view about the appropriate defensive posture a country must take-and it is our view about NATO and some other positions-it is our firm desire to reduce tension in the world and to reduce the need to resort to military defence. That is the position which this Party has consistently supported. That is why we support this proposal, at least in its conceptual form. We believe deeply that we cannot simply attain disarmament or a lack of tension by saying that we want it. We have to do what we believe is necessary in the time and place. At the same time we have to find some way to create dialogue, a reduction of tension and a conflict resolution which will make it possible for all countries in the world to reduce their arms build-up and their reliance upon military measures.
I see no conflict, as the Hon. Member may, between our support for matters which relate to current situations of conflict and crisis and our desire to find a way to reduce the underlying tensions which lead to those conflicts. What we are saying here is that the importance of peace can never be over-estimated. We want to take whatever steps or measures we can to ensure that the institute created to inch us back, as the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) indicated, from the nuclear chasm will work. That is what we are trying to say today.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member for a clarification of the word "independence". I have great concerns about this particular organization. I feel very strongly that it should go through, and I will be speaking on it in a few minutes. The independence I am worried about is that it be completely independent of Government Departments such as the Department of National Defence or the Department of External Affairs and that it functions independently in that way.
I am beginning to get the feeling that the Hon. Member is talking about political independence, that it be sort of non-partisan. I think it should be too, but I am wondering whether the Hon. Member is thinking about both kinds of independence, whether it be a Liberal thing, a Tory thing or something like that, or whether basically he is thinking about an organization that is quite independent of other parts of government in terms of coming to its own decisions. This kind of independence is crucial, and I think the other kind of independence can be easily worked out in the way we work out the Bill. However, there are two different kinds of independence. I would like the Hon. Member to distinguish between one or the other. Perhaps the Hon. Member could indicate whether he is in favour of
April 17, 1984

this organization functioning without being dependent upon other organs or departments of government.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I would be happy to try to answer the question. As I understand the system, Departments report to Ministers and Ministers are responsible for Departments. Therefore I find the concept of distinguishing between independence of Departments and independence of Ministries to be a null distinction.
If I may put it in a context which I know better, we believe that no Minister of the Crown of any political stripe, including our own, should have the right to tell the institute what it must research or to create an impression in the mind of the institute that it must do something in order to obtain the Minister's blessing.
If I wanted to put a parallel to the Hon. Member, it would be this one. For a series of extremely good reasons, we have over the years granted the Canada Council maximum possible independence from ministerial control, from governmental control and from departmental control, so that when it makes grants to people in the artistic community it is to the greatest possible degree seen to be acting independently of governmental, political or departmental control. I believe we are espousing that exact principle in terms of our proposals with regard to this institute. I repeat that we want this institute to be seen to be and to be independent of departmental, ministerial and political control, not for the sake of the government of the day but for the quality of research which will result given that independence.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I want to be clear so that he knows I make no particular fuss about the institute doing some of its own research. However, I have a concern in terms of the academic institutions of the country, if the new direction for research is seen to be that the Government creates an industry which uses government research money to do research exclusively. My instinctive reaction would be that I think to the greatest degree possible we have two opportunities here. One is to increase the amount of money directed at "peace research". The second is to use that money to support institutions specializing in research by directing to the greatest practical degree possible the talent and resources to do the research and by asking the agency to do as much as it can in institutions which conduct
International Peace and Security research and to restrict its inhouse research activities to those areas where it has no other choice.
That is what I am trying to get at. I believe we would be risking support in the academic communities if we said that the Government's intention was to move its research funds exclusively into the area of inhouse research.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Order, please. For debate, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae).

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I am very pleased to participate in this debate because I feel there is a great degree of urgency in establishing this institute. On a number of occasions I have written to and spoken with members of the Government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and so on, about the need for a very independent institute to conduct studies in peace and security. I am delighted we have finally arrived at the point where we can get around to establishing this institute. I hope there will be no difficulty and that in the next month or so we will be able to put it together and have it operating certainly by the summer.
I attended a meeting of 500 or 600 people in Toronto a couple of weeks ago at which United States Admiral Carroll was the speaker. He was asked about how much time he felt we had before a war would occur, or if a war would occur. His answer was that yes it would in about eight years and that the basic growth of very, very dangerous weapons and the attitudes of the two superpowers were such that this was a very real possibility.
This is something about which I have been very apprehensive. I find it difficult to accept that the House has spent so little time on this most important of all issues. We have a situation today where there are in excess of 50,000 nuclear weapons, nuclear warheads, that are pretty well distributed. There is a little more on our side than on the Soviet side, but theirs are larger ones. One way or another, there is an area where we have general parity. What I mean by general parity is that each side has the capability of destroying the other side almost completely and then being destroyed themselves. No one side could destroy the other side without they themselves being destroyed as well. That is the situation we are faced with.
There is in existence today something like 5,000 times the explosive power that was used in all of World War II. I simply do not understand those who say that we are not strong enough and need to build more arms. It is completely beyond my comprehension that we need more arms when we already have
5,000	times the fire power that was available in World War II.
We are told by some very eminent scientists on both sides of the Iron Curtain that we need to worry about more than just the explosive effects of these weapons. In total, these weapons have 100,000 times the destructive power of the weapons that destroyed Hiroshima. We have the situation of the explosive power and the nuclear fallout which, if the bomb did not hit Canada, would still kill about 12 million Canadians. More

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security people from my own community of Thunder Bay would die than died in all of Canada during World War I and World War II. However, in addition to this, we are told by these eminent scientists that the effect of these explosions, even if only a small portion of them were used, would be to create a nuclear winter which would probably destroy most of the plant life in the northern hemisphere. Millions and millions of Canadians would then die from the cold and from famine. Civilization as we know it would cease to exist. Yet a retired American admiral, along with his friends, retired American generals and admirals, are saying that this can happen and that it can happen within the next seven or eight years. It can happen because the weaponry that is being built at this particular time can create a situation in which this can happen simply through computer error.
I would remind the House that as we sit here this very moment, a few Pershing II missiles have been installed in West Germany which have a six-minute to eight-minute time span between firing and destroying a target in the Soviet Union. The Soviets tell us that they now have weapons based six to eight minutes from the shore of the United States. We find ourselves in a situation in which a computer error could result in a mistaken firing which could result in return firing and a launch-on warning. This is the situation today and it is only beginning. It will become much worse. Shorter trajectory times and greater accuracy will be built into many weapons and the threat of a pre-emptive or first strike could cause the other side to strike in a crisis. These are the situations which exist today. It is possible that the world could be destroyed within 30 minutes.
It is absolutely essential that Canadians and people all over the world do whatever is possible to make sure that this kind of destruction is prevented. This is the reason why I support the need for this Bill. If we are to be successful as peace makers, then we must have access to good, solid, objective information. We should not have information from only one source like the Pentagon or another source like Soviet publications but we need good, solid information from all sources. There is an organization in Sweden called SIPRI which is set up to provide this kind of information. In the research I have done over the last three or four years, I have found that the information from that source has been very valuable to us in assessing the claims of both sides.
We have a situation where one side is saying the other side is superior and vice versa. Of course, all of the information available to me and the information from other sources like the Scowcroft Commission would point to the fact that there is no superiority, that we are in a situation of general parity and that now is the time to slow things down.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has done a great deal of travelling and has spoken to a great many leaders all over the world. He made a speech in the House on February 9 and came to the conclusion that there are about 10 major ideas which are common to the superpowers. We should begin to work with those common ideas. I will not deal with all of those ideas because I have only 20 minutes in which to speak, but I
will mention two or three of them. One such idea is the agreement that a nuclear war cannot be fought and cannot be won. There is agreement that we must get rid of destabilizing weapons and there is agreement that the other side exists, will continue to exist and that there should not be an attempt to depose the other side. These ideas are very vital and were common threads which ran through all of the discussions the Prime Minister had with all of the world leaders including the leaders of both superpowers.
In order to make these common ideas work, we must know what we are doing. We must have access to good, independent information. It seems to me that there is a very direct relationship between the kind of thing the Prime Minister and others throughout the world have been attempting to do and the kind of thing that we hope to do with this Bill. I am particularly interested in seeing that, through this Bill, we set up an independent organization. To me, an independent organization means one which will not rely only on the Department of National Defence or the Department of External Affairs. An independent organization will not follow only the demands of those two Departments.
I would agree entirely with Members of the Opposition and particularly with the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) who said that from Clause 28 of the Bill, the word "shall" should be removed. I think the Prime Minister as well agreed with that. If not, the Department of External Affairs and the Department of National Defence could very well ask this organization to respond in a certain way or to do a certain study. That is a legitimate request, but certainly the obligation to do such a study will not, in my opinion, give the organization the kind of independence it needs. I think that the word "may" is probably more applicable to the situation.
I would disagree with the Hon. Member from the NDP who suggested that that clause should be removed entirely. I believe that the word "may" at least indicates that the Department cannot force certain things on this organization. If the clause were not included in the Bill at all, there might be some assumption that the organization could be forced by the Department to do things. I think it would be just as well to leave Clause 28 in place and replace the word "shall" with the word "may". I think that would give to the organization the kind of independence it needs.
I spent some time looking at what they are doing at the Swedish peace institute in Stockholm. I looked at the structure of that institute and I believe that this is a model at which we should all take a good look. That institute has established itself in a number of basic areas and, in my opinion, a number of things about the structure of that organization give it a great deal of independence and the kind of independence we would like to have here in Canada.
First, that institute is funded by the Government and not by the private sector. I would not object to private-sector funding for various peace institutes, but I think the institute to which the Bill refers must be funded by the Government partly because there is a need for credibility when dealing with both sides. If we are to study Soviet-American relations, we must be
April 17, 1984

credible to both those groups. We must have an organization with that kind of credibility. If we are dealing with the Soviets, we will not be credible if the foundation is a legitimate one but is funded by large corporations from the private sector. It is important that we do it this way. It does not mean that other organizations, peace groups and study groups should not be funded by the private sector. This is one area where it is important that the funding come this way.
I may be running into some problems with the Opposition on this, but the Swedish Institute has an international board. It includes people from Sweden and also has an international component. I disagree with the Hon. Member for New West-minster-Coquitlam (Miss Jewett) who spoke about keeping this institute Canadian. I have had a great deal to do with the peace movement over the last few years, the last three years in particular. One of the dangers is the tendency to become pure, just to worry about what Canadians are doing, making sure that we are pure, not doing anything wrong and in no way contributing to nuclear armament, not worrying about what is going on outside.
I have had a great deal of concern about the testing of the Cruise. If this testing does not take place in Canada, it will take place somewhere else. It does not make much difference where it has been tested if a war should occur. It is important in terms of how we feel about ourselves.
It is nice to advocate that Canada be a nuclear free zone. We can feel good about that. However, if there is a nuclear war, we will be in the centre of it. It will come to us. If we declare that we are nuclear free, that does not mean we will not have to worry about the war.
I feel that Canadians are becoming a little bit too concerned about appearing pure rather than being concerned about preventing a war between the superpowers. Therefore, it would be a mistake if the board were to be entirely Canadian. It requires an international flavour. I believe that the structure of the board should include Canadians and a number of people from other countries. That is tremendously important. If we are serious about preventing nuclear war, we must have an organization with global concerns. We cannot solve the problem just by being pure. We have to be concerned about the two superpowers and how they can be brought together.
While we have talked about the structure of this organization, we have not talked about its role. Earlier I referred to the 10 points which the Prime Minister presented as areas where we could get agreement. Canadians have to focus on the nature of the two superpowers.
We are very close to the United States and know a great deal about it. Many of us worry about the present U.S. Government. We feel the worries would go away if the Democrats were in power. At least that is my feeling. Basically we understand the situation. We understand some of what has to be done to bring the two superpowers together. We do not have a good understanding about the Soviet Union. We do not understand them. Their ideologies are different from ours. We
International Peace and Security tend not to want to know very much about them, what they are like and what their Government stands for. We have a situation where it is impossible to destroy that Government. It is not possible to do very much to change that Government. We have to understand their Government and the people there.
I hope the institute is set up fairly soon because the situation between the two powers is critical. Basically they are not speaking to each other. There are some talks going on in Stockholm. They are going on not too badly, partly because the superpowers are surrounded by other powers, including ourselves. They are not really confronting each other in areas where they should be talking.
If we develop these studies, particularly in the area of understanding the superpowers, we can use this information to bring other middle powers together and develop a negotiating team which could work between the two superpowers to reduce the tension. This could be done along the lines suggested by the Prime Minister, beginning in areas of common interest, concern and agreement. There are the 10 points, and others could be added to the list. If we could learn how to deal with them, if we could have ideas through third power groups, possibly we could bring some kind of sanity to the two superpowers.
If we do not do this in the next few years, then Admiral Carroll and other knowledgeable people on the subject will be correct that a nuclear war, which has never occurred in the history of mankind, will take place and we will be destroyed. The stakes are so great that this is absolutely essential. Even though it is a small step, we should take it, pass this Bill and set up a good independent organization.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened to the Hon. Member quite closely. Several times he said how important he felt it was that the organization should be independent. Will he indicate if he feels in that context that it should be a government institution?

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought about this a good deal. I have been saying that it should be independent in the sense that it cannot be set up in such a way that the individual Departments, particularly DND and External Affairs which are the two most vitally concerned, have a strong influence on either the day to day or long-term operation. This is tremendously important. This is why I strongly support the Conservative amendment that will replace the word "shall" with the word "may". The problem that I see from the speeches we have heard today is that this could be done on a partisan basis. I do not want to see that. It does not have anything to do with partisanship. I do not see how we can set up this institute, without some government action. The point is that we have to do this together. The word "consultation" has to be worked as it has never worked before in terms of how we set up this organization. Who is on the board is terribly important. You can have the best structure in the world but if the people in it do not want to succeed, you will not achieve anything. That is

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security terribly important. I believe, through the workings of the committee and so on, we can get to a point where we can be pretty independent in the way it is structured. Once it is set up on its own then I feel it is terribly important that it be set up in such a way that it cannot be influenced at any given stage. That is why I feel that word "may" is important. It is important to leave "may" in there. It should not be taken out as an Hon. Member suggested earlier, because if it is taken out there could be some suggestion that the word "shall', would be quietly implied. We know that the word "may" means that the organization itself can reject any suggestions of the Government. It seems to me that is the key point.
As far as setting up this institute is concerned, I believe one has to go along with the notion that there is an executive in every government. A Party which hopes, and I suppose expects, to come to power in the next little while is going to find that the executive has to act. However, I believe there is no difficulty in this situation if we are all concerned, and I know we are. I know Hon. Members who spoke this morning are very concerned.

speechtext: I suppose if the issue had arisen a year or so before, and if the Prime Minister's moves had been made a year or two earlier-and I believe the Prime Minister's moves had a lot to do with a number of factors-I feel it would have been nice to get this thing going before. Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the previous speaker to give us his thoughts on the internationalization of the directors of the board of governors. He seemed to make quite a point of that. Is that related to the
April 17, 1984

role he sees Canada playing as the honest broker or mediator in trying to resolve the problems of East-West relations?

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe that is precisely what I had in mind. However, I do not mean that Canada alone is going to do this. It seems to me that we can participate. In the first place, just geographically we are sitting between the two superpowers. We are sort of the meat in the sandwich, if you will. We must have good studies going on. I believe also that the international board will give us an ability to function in a larger arena. More than anything I was worried about the fact that we would become just Canadians and look upon the solution with the idea that as long as we are pure, everything else will be fine. I believe there is a very strong role to be played by the country which sits between the two superpowers.

As you will recall, the main thrust of my question was whether the Hon. Member felt that this new peace institute should be a government organization. subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just do not quite follow the line of questioning. I understand what I have been asked but I am not so sure that I understand what the Hon. Member is attempting to get at. There are various kinds of government organizations, some of them fairly close to the Departments where they function, some at arm's length. For example, the IDRC is a fairly independent organization. What I am saying is that it has to be a body which is independent of government Departments. The degree of independence is the crucial point. There must be a way of funding so that once the institute is on its own it will function independently. But it is still a government organization.
I hope the Hon. Member is not suggesting that it should be funded by the private sector as some kind of a foundation. That is not what I want. I want this to be a government-funded organization but with the Government at arm's length.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Member then agree that the Library of Parliament might be a better model in that it is responsible to the Speakers of this and the other place, as well as to a joint committee, and is funded by a direct appropriation from Parliament? In short, it answers to Parliament, not to the Government of the day.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not thought of that particular model. It seems to me we could look at it. That might very well be just as easy, although if you had an endowment it might be simpler.
If a Government is in power-and the Hon. Member and his colleagues beleive they may at some point come into power- the Government tends to direct Parliament. We are a parliamentary system, not a Republican system where you have separate executive and legislative branches. It seems to me that even though we are a parliamentary system, there would be quite an independent approach through the committee. Fundamentally, in our system the Government has to be in charge. If we want to change the system, that is a whole different ball game, but the Government tends to be in charge of Parliament. It has the votes to do what it has to do. Therefore, I just wonder if we are getting into something that does not mean very much.

speechtext:
The other remark he made, which leads me into the main part of my speech, was that this institute could not and should not duplicate work done abroad. There are an awful lot of institutions in the world, 264 by count, which do work similarly to what we envisage. Most consider themselves to be international institutes. I noticed that the title of the Bill puts the word "international" in a different place in the sentence. It says, "the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security", whereas a world-famous institute calls itself the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
I notice the U.S. has 60 or 70 of these institutions. Some are more prominent than others, and most are prominent because they have established a record of precise, objective work. Everything else tends to fail in this field or else becomes the Bible of single purpose groups who can read what they want to read in some of the inferior books and papers published by the lesser known institutions.
I would like to speak for a moment about the International Institute for Strategic Studies. If we are going to have an institute that is supposed to study international affairs, I believe that we should have a good one. It is difficult for me to understand at the present time exactly what the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security is going to do, what its main role is going to be and what its subsidiary roles will be. They seem to change with every speaker. I think the International Institute for Strategic Studies is the top institute of its kind in the world. That institute says it has three major functions: research, information and debate. They put out some publications, namely, The Military Balance, Strategic Survey, Adelphi Papers and Survival. These come out as
April 17, 1984

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security choosing of the people involved. For example, the Bill states that:
The Directors ... shall be appointed by the Governor in Council to hold office for such term not exceeding three years as will ensure as far as possible the expiration in any one year of the terms of fewer than half of the directors so appointed.
This is probably the exact same thing that covers the board which is appointed by the Governor in Council to run Cana-dair and de Havilland. Those are government boards appointed for running organizations which they know nothing about. If that is the way it will be, there will be one extremely important person and it will not be the chairman, who will also be appointed by the Governor in Council. I shudder to think of some of the people the Government might pick.
The executive director is the chief executive officer of the institute. He is also appointed by the Governor in Council. His function is to run the organization and hire the staff. What kind of staff would there be if the executive officer was the Hon. J. P. Goyer or someone like that? I am very concerned about that position and the fact that there will be no input unless one is a Cabinet Minister in the current Government.
I very much favour this amendment taking the selection of these people out of the hands of the Cabinet and giving it either to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence or a meeting of the House of Commons where the various options could be presented to us.
The Vice-Chairman will be elected by the board. Clause 10 states:
The Board shall elect one of the directors, other than the Executive Director, to be Vice-Chairman of the Board.
According to this Bill, that is the only duty given to the board. After they elect the vice-chairman, they can go back to wherever they came from while the executive director continues to run the firm on direction from the Cabinet. I do not believe that that is the proper procedure.
I would prefer that the Bill be changed. While the purpose of the Bill is exactly what we need, in order to have a world class organization we must be very careful about how it will be structured, how people will be selected and what their terms of office will be. Will they have independence from the Cabinet? I do not believe that Canadair has independence from the Cabinet or from the Minister of Transport. I doubt very much that the provisions of this Bill will permit the organization to have independence from the Minister of National Defence and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The directors themselves have a sinecure that might make them happy, but I do not think it will do much to increase the knowledge of Canadians about External Affairs at the present time.
I believe the only two items of importance in Clause 4 which lists the purposes are Clause 4(1) to "collect and disseminate information and ideas on international peace and security", and Clause 4(d) to "foster, fund and conduct research on international peace and security issues of particular interest to Canadians or to the Government of Canada". These are
strange words to use. How can matters be of particular interest to Canadians when we are talking about world peace? It is rather difficult for me to understand.
I am also totally baffled by the funding of this institute. While there is provision for $1.5 million in the coming year, which is to go up to $5 million, I notice that a small section of Clause 5 provides that the institute also have the authority to acquire any property, money or securities by gift, bequest or otherwise. Presumably this means that it would be open to public funding, if someone wished to contribute money to it. I am not sure whether in hard years the Government might not use that provision as a barometer and cut down on government funding and tell the institute that it would have to do as the local museum does and raise money on its own. It is not satisfactory to allow the possibility of public funding without responsibility for deciding whether it will use it or not.
My main concern lies with the selection of officers. We would like to have it taken out of Cabinet hands, particularly at this stage in our political life when an election is coming, whether the Government wants it or not. It is not the time to leave behind three years' worth of political hacks for the rest of us to deal with.

Mr. Speaker, my objection to the funding as provided for in this Bill concerns the vagueness of the clause which permits it to acquire property, money or securities by gift, bequest or otherwise. subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY

Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat puzzled by the remarks made by the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) earlier today and subsequently by the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley). I would like to understand what proposition is being put forward by the Hon. Members of the Official Opposition about how this factor of independence can best be achieved, given the fact that we have the British parliamentary form of government, known otherwise as responsible government.
Would the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) tell us what he believes could be an alternative organism to Cabinet for appointing the chairman, board of directors and executive director of this institution? I say that not in an argumentative sense. I say it because I have sat here today and I would love to understand what alternative option is available and justifiably available. If the Hon. Member is suggesting that it would require the Members of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence to make an appointment of the executive or the board of directors and chairman of this institution and then he refers to a consensus, I begin to lose track of what he means. I do not know of a system of parliament or a system of government, either one of them, that has been used in that sense. I have never heard of that type of appointment system before. I would love to be educated on it.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the Hon. Member about his confusion with the word consensus. He has not had an opportunity to find out, but Cabinet committees operate on consensus. Although that itself bears some argument at times as to what a consensus is. It is generally thought of as being very close to totality, but not necessarily so. It keeps individuals from having a veto in committees.
International Peace and Security
As far as the funding goes and the organization that should look after this, recommendations have been made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) to the Prime Minister, and I understand a recommendation by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). I am not privileged to divulge them. This afternoon the Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) made a suggestion that the institute could operate in the way the Parliamentary Library does, which is operating, as far as this side is concerned, very, very well indeed. The Library has a good executive director. He picks a good staff and they do well. I cannot see any reason why we could not do the same with this proposed institute.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) not understand that funding for the Library of Parliament is accessed through the Standing Committee on Management and Members' Services? The fact is that the Library is run under the management of the Commissioners of Internal Economy, all of whom are Cabinet Ministers. That is our principle of responsible government. How does the Hon. Member propose to fund this committee? How does he propose to appoint members to this institution? How does the Hon. Member propose to run it? The example he gives confirms perfectly that in a responsible sense of British parliamentary democracy it is Cabinet Ministers who have to dispose of funds. Now the Hon. Member is proposing some committee of the House of Commons-or should we perhaps ask the Library of Parliament research committee whether or not it feels it should fund the peace institute? We would like a little clarity if we could.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is not my duty to write Bills because the Government is unable to write one that is satisfactory to Parliament. I think the group on this side of the House would prefer to have as much independence as possible for this institute. We feel that it would be absolutely impossible for the institute to have its independence if we go along with this Bill, which will give the Cabinet an ability to put its finger into the business of the institute at any time it wants. Indeed, there is a particular exception for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. If the Secretary of State for External Affairs can tell the institute what to do and if he wants some advice on any area or subject, he can insist the institute do it. That is the kind of interference we really do not want.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: You do not want the Minister to be enlightened?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Order, please. For debate, the Hon. Member for Esquimalt-Saanich.

subtopic: CANADIAN INSTITUTE FOR INTERNATIONAL PEACE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my intervention this afternoon will consist mainly of probing the Government to find answers to questions that are not satisfactorily answered in the Bill as it now stands. I think that is a very proper procedure on second reading. There are matters here and there will be comment and criticism as well of the Bill as it stands. But also, at least in the first part of my intervention, there will be some inquiries as to where the

April 17, 1984
International Peace and Security
Government thinks it is going with this institute and why it is doing it at this time.
That, indeed, is my first question. It is a question of timing. Why in the spring of 1984 in Canada, in Holy Week, has this matter been brought before the House of Commons? I have heard it said that Holy Week is considered in some church circles as the week of peace. That is a very appropriate stance for the churches to take at this particular season of the church year. I do wonder, however, whether the Government is trying to come under this umbrella and make use of that particular time of year to sneak in its proposals about a peace institute.
The other question that comes to my mind, and I do not know whether I will ever get an answer to it, is whether there is some relationship between the introduction of this Bill now when the Government is talking about June 16 as a deadline for its completion and the retirement of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). Or whether there is a thought in somebody's mind that maybe the present Prime Minister should be the chairman or the executive director of this institute as a form of occupation after he ceases to be the Prime Minister of Canada. Is that what lies behind the timing of this Bill? I think the whole country is interested in that. That matter of peace has been before the world for centuries. I venture to suggest that those of us who have worn uniforms are the strongest advocates of peace. Those who know and those who have been under fire know what peace is and what peace means. We would like to see peace. I wonder also about the political implications of the timing, because it has been my experience that very little is done by this Government that does not have some political overtones, either to discomfort the Opposition or to further its own cause with the electorate at this time. There is an election coming. I think peace, a peace institute and the concept of peace are much too valuable to play with in this way. I suspect, nonetheless, that there is an element of politics in this, a very strong element.
What about the economic climate in which this matter is being introduced? Is this just a smoke-screen so that the problems of unemployment can be forgotten and put aside for a time? What about the problems of the economy, the national debt and inflation? These matters that affect the lives of so many Canadians, are they being put to one side, obfuscated and made less clear by this particular introduction? There were other times when this particular matter could have been brought forward.
I gather from the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) that he has some notion that this institute is going to achieve peace in the world, that somehow or other Canada will act as the intermediary, the honest broker, the mediator between East and West through the medium of this institution and I wonder whether that is what the Government has in mind.
The other question which I have to ask myself I will ask aloud in the hopes that there will be a reply from the government side. It concerns the matter of haste. Why are we trying
to rush through this matter just now? However, before dealing with that, there is one element which confuses me-the shift in emphasis in the title of this particular institute from the notion in the Speech from the Throne that this particular matter would be brought forward. We have heard the Speech from the Throne quoted before wherein it indicates:
-the Government will create a publicly funded centre to gather, collate and digest the enormous volume of information now available on defence and arms control issues.
It went on further to indicate:
The Government will increase its funding for voluntary associations and private research groups interested in security, arms control and disarmament issues. Resources for research and development of verification procedures, the basis of successful arms control agreements, will be expanded substantially.
The emphasis in the Throne Speech was upon defence, arms control verification and disarmament. The word "security" appeared there, and now we find it transmogrified or shifted in some manner or other and it has come out as the establishment of the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. Obviously there is a relationship between disarmament, international peace and security. Also there is a relationship-and I say this in pure objectivity-between armament and security. Therefore I find myself somewhat mystified by the shift in the wording as it appeared in the Throne Speech to the title as it now stands. I wonder whether this change of emphasis from the original purpose is intended to establish the linkage between defence and security, for example, or the linkage between arms control and international peace. What is it that underlies this shift of emphasis?
I think the Government owes Parliament an answer on that. I think it also owes the Canadian public an answer. The answers to these questions were not fully laid out by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) in his opening remarks. I listened carefully to see whether he would establish that. Somewhere along the line, perhaps in committee or if the Minister intervenes at some time, we should be able to probe this particular matter and discover what motivated the Government to change its mind in this way.
I mentioned earlier the matter of the haste with which we are now being asked to consider this Bill. Timing is one thing, and I have mentioned that already, but the urge to get the institute set up and operating as soon as possible is another. That is a matter of haste. Why the haste? What lies behind the need to have this institute set up?
Some notion was expressed somewhere or other that the committee to which the Bill will be referred should examine this matter in a matter of a week or so. Mr. Speaker, do you know how many institutes and concerned people there are in this country who are concerned with peace and will want to make representations to the committee? I do not understand how the Government considers it possible between now and June 16-and the mysticism surrounding this particular date escapes me-for this institute, with all the flaws in the Bill, to become fact.
April 17, 1984

It is vitally important that the hearings before the standing committee be of sufficient duration to obtain the input of all interested and involved Canadians, be they individuals, the academic community or organized groups of one kind or another. I am sure the Council of Bishops would be interested in making representations, urging changes and urging that the institute be set up. I will not speak for that Council, but many organizations will want to make representations to the committee. I think a full opportunity should be provided to them for that purpose. It would be an error of prime importance if there was any intention to let the axe fall on these hearings or on the discussions of this particular Bill.
I urge that there be no precipitated or under-considered action on this matter. Perhaps it is possible to be consistent with the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan. Perhaps what is needed is a Canadian centre for East-West studies so that we could understand the problem and get to the root, in Canadian terms, of some of our troubles. When the Bill goes before it, the committee should be allowed to hear the matters fully, not cut off debate.
I would like to turn to the purpose of the institute as set out in the Bill. Aside from the uncertainty created by the confusion concerning peace and security on the one hand and defence, arms control and disarmament on the other, with which I have already dealt, there is or ought to be a strictly Canadian emphasis in the purpose of the Bill. We are all exploring. The Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) mentioned the need for internationalization. 1 happen to feel that there is a very strong argument in favour of Canadianiza-tion and the insistence thereon. In fact, if we look at Clause 4(d) of the Bill, we find that research on international peace and security issues which the institute is to undertake shall be "of particular interest to Canadians or to the Government of Canada". I think that is most important. After all, we are part of the Parliament of Canada. Surely it is in our interests to ensure that Canadians, the Government and all institutions in Canada are aware of the issues involved in this matter. Clause 18 leaves open the national bias of directors. I find that just a little odd, but I will return to it if I have the opportunity. Clause 18 reads:
The Chairman, Executive Director and at least eight of the other directors of the Board must be Canadian citizens.
This leaves open the possibility of appointing seven non-Canadians to the board of governors. I tried to find out from the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan what he had in mind and why he felt it was so essential that the directors be internationalized. Unfortunately, I did not receive a satisfactory answer. I myself am not clear in my mind why that should be.
I wonder if the Government will ever let us know what kind of people it has in mind for this board. Are academics, retired public servants, retired Prime Ministers, retired Cabinet Ministers or unelected former Cabinet Ministers to be nominated to this board of governors? I believe it is time we had some
International Peace and Security
clarification on that matter. I mentioned a few people in the international field who might be in the Prime Minister's mind.
I do not know whether it might be the former Prime Minister of Jamaica, Georgi Arbatov of the Soviet Union or anyone else. However, I think the time has come when the Government should give us some indication of whom they have in mind for appointments to these other seven positions.
How is such a board to preserve the Canadian focus of which I spoke a few moments ago? How will it focus on Canada's interests? The names of the people to be nominated are not forthcoming. We do not know what kind of Canadians the Government has in mind let alone what kind of non-Canadians.
I turn now to another very important matter which has been the object of the concerns of all our speakers, and that is, the independence of this institute from Government and its accountability to Parliament. I did not receive a copy of the Bill until last evening but I went through it fairly carefully and I was a little worried by the lack of independence provided for the institute by the Bill. I will turn to the lack of accountability in a moment.
I was struck forcibly by the comments of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) this morning when he drew the attention of the House to Clauses 25 and 26 of the Bill. I had missed those clauses when I read the Bill last evening. Those who missed those clauses might well consider the words of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead. Clause 25 of the Bill reads as follows:
The Board shall, forthwith after making a by-law, send a copy thereof to the Minister and the President of the Treasury Board.
Why should such a copy not be sent to Parliament as well? I do not think that that matter is too troublesome. However, Clause 26 reads:
The Governor in Council may, by order, direct the Board to make, amend or repeal a by-law within such period as is specified in the order.
Is this independence of the Government, Mr. Speaker? I would ask the Minister that question to his face. Is this what he conceives as being independence of the institute from Government? As well, Clause 27 is relevant to the matter of independence.
I believe that it is absolutely essential that this institute be independent. There should be no question about its independence. There is a means of ensuring this. I believe it was the Hon. Member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker) who asked how independence could be secured by the process of having the standing committee approve proposed directors. DAILY NEWSPAPER ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-226, an Act to ensure, at the national level, competition and independence of the daily press, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity, my first chance to put forward a Bill in Private Members' hour for some years. It is a very important issue for discussion this afternoon. Always the optimist as a Member of the House of Commons for some 11 years, I hope that it might gain support from all sides of the House, or at least go to a vote. I will not
April 17, 1984

waste a lot of time pleading that case, knowing tradition during this hour.
This Bill is entitled "an Act to ensure, at the national level, competition and independence of the daily press". The Bill is essentially a carbon copy of a Cabinet-approved Bill put forward during this Parliament in response to the royal commission on newspapers in Canada. The only exception is the exclusion of the part of the Bill dealing with a national newspaper advisory council, its establishment and the creation of an endowment fund, and within that same section the offering of matching grants of up to $50,000 for up to three years for daily newspapers in Canada which would open up new bureaus outside of the region in which they are located or outside of Canada and reporting back to Canada.
I say that for clarification as I begin to make my presentation on this Bill. First, as we all know, Private Members' Bills are not allowed to put forward the expenditure of money. This removes that possibility. I might say that we do have across Canada, since the report of the royal commission and the proposals by the Government that followed at that time, the development of volunteer press councils across this country. Previously there were only press councils in Ontario, Quebec and Alberta. Frankly, in Ontario, less than half the daily newspapers with far less than half the daily circulation belonged at that time. Now almost all daily newspapers in Ontario belong and almost all in Quebec. Indeed, we now have a council for the Maritime provinces, a council for Alberta and Saskatchewan, a new council in Manitoba and a new council in British Columbia.
I am heartened by that, although I am still concerned about the issue of credibility of those press councils. They are largely funded by the publishers. The first set of appointments to those councils are made by the publishers. Often editorials and journalists suggest that we must not show either a conflict of interest or a perceived conflict of interest. Therefore, I see some problem with that credibility. The proof will be in how they perform. I want to be an optimist on that. When so many of our Canadian cities have only one daily newspaper, at least there is a place where individuals can go to vet their grievances.
In the case of the grants, which are not included in this legislation but were in the proposed daily newspaper Bill, there was a great deal of hyperbole from the newspaper industry about how they would not accept money from the federal Government, how that would somehow be government trying to get into the newsrooms of the nations. I found that absurd. There is no excise tax on newspapers. That is an allowance of government which saves newspapers in Canada many millions of dollars. The press facilities on Parliament Hill must cost many tens if not hundreds of thousands of dollars. They are used without question. I certainly do not see the press being bought off by having those facilities. There are postal subsidies which are of assistance today, particularly in western Canada, in helping some dailies reach their customers.
The complaint against the grants is a bit hollow. At least as I pass that part and note that it is not included because of the
Daily Newspaper Act
costs involved and therefore not allowed in a Private Members' Bill, I make the point that the Kent Royal Commission found, and I very much agree with it that, sadly, in this country there is very little reporting from one region to another. Out of that comes our continuing lack of understanding of each other as Canadians. When we count so much on our place in the international scene, and certainly 25 per cent of our Gross National Product relates to exports, we should have more Canadians in key centres around the world and experts on Canada reporting back to us.
I now want to move to the two major issues which are included in what is left of this Bill, which is almost word for word the same as the previously proposed Cabinet-approved daily newspaper Act. Those two major issues are the issue of concentration of ownership of daily newspapers in Canada. The second is to establish in principle for future purposes in the starting up of newspapers editorial independence from other interests.
First let me deal with the issue of concentration. In English Canada two chains, Thompson and Southam, now control almost two-thirds of daily newspaper circulation. They have arrived there within the law. That is not my attack. That level of concentration, as I will try to argue over the next few minutes, can have a critical effect upon what a free press must be in a democracy like ours.
Second, in French speaking Canada the concentration level by chains is 90 per cent or more, the difference being that in Quebec most of those chains are in head-to-head competition with each other. In the case of English speaking Canada, those two chains generally have exclusively to themselves, one or the other, a particular daily newspaper marketplace.
I believe at the national level, when we now have a higher level of concentration in this country than in any other democracy in the western world, a level of concentration of ownership four times as large as that in the United States, surely the time has come when we must stop this and encourage more competition.
When we use the famous phrase of free press, some publishers and indeed editorialists believe that it means it is free for them to use as they see fit. Indeed, that is an element, but finally and essentially a free press belongs to individual Canadians. Canadians have a right to a whole diversity of views and expressions of newspapers and information available for them to make their judgment on society at the local, provincial and national levels. A free press is the right of individual Canadians and of our society, not a right of parliamentarians, government or the publishers. It is a right of the people.
The free press must be diverse in order that we will have competing sources. Competing sources of information means a number of things. It means that journalists have mobility. If there are only one or two big bosses to work for, your boss does not like what you are doing, you feel in conscience you are honestly reporting something and you know there are not many other places to get a job, that may well hamper your ability to be an independent and outspoken journalist.
3162

without a phone call from head office saying, "Do not report on our labour disputes" or "Do not report on the criticism of the machines we turn out in another part of this company", just by the very knowledge that head office also has those other interests, the story might not be reported or as well reported. That was a major concern of the Kent Commission.
The proposal in this Bill is that if someone who is largely not in the information business is going to buy a newspaper or start up a newspaper, they would simply have to go to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission and demonstrate how they would ensure that that editorial room was independent of other interests. The penalties are not great because we only have the right to inquire. But that public focus, that need to be judged so that the public can point the finger and say, "Indeed, that is your intention," the independence that that would give to such an editorial operation seems to me to be very important, and it is totally absent from the proposed new combines legislation.
I also want to note that during my time as Minister responsible for the government reaction to the royal commission, the indignation of most of the publishers, in my view, approached the ridiculous. Concerns about concentration of press ownership have been tackled by most western democracies. I mentioned earlier some detail on that. That includes Britain, Germany, France, Italy and even the United States. Therefore, we quiver and shake and say, "Politicians, keep your hands off newspapers". I agree that no government, no politician, should have the ability to impact on or influence the editorial room, the news room. On the other hand, Parliament should not stand back when concentration of ownership, by the admission of all the publishers I have spoken to, has reached a point when that concentration of ownership can become dangerous, although they would not say exactly what that level was. When concentration endangers the free flow of information, diversity, accuracy, the mobility of reporters, then surely it is the responsibility of parliamentarians to act.
Royal Assent
individual Canadians, in all their diversity and with all their need for and right to diverse information and views.
Parliament works because the system forces us to keep each other on our toes, open to competing views, positions and criticisms. That same pressure of competition and competing views is essential for the maintenance of a free press. Newspapers are special. They set the news agenda. They are more permanent. They are the printed record and have a special credibility. To ignore what has been happening in the Canadian newspaper industry, to bend to the vocal, powerful and largely self-serving few who already dominate, is to invite a weaker and a poorer democracy. I urge you all, my colleagues in this House, each of us as Private Member, to support this Bill and the fundamental freedom it is attempting to protect.
