speakeroldname: Mr. Michel Veillette (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: DAILY NEWSPAPER ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we cannot remain silent about the historical background of this Bill. The Government has been interested in the newspaper industry for many years now. Hon. Members may remember, first the 1971 Senate report on mass media and, more recently, the Kent Royal Commission on Newspapers which reported to the Government. As a result of that report, the Hon. Member made public in July 1983 a series of recommendations aimed at regulating concentration and conduct in the newspaper industry. The purpose of those recommendations was to elicit public reaction and to draft appropriate legislative measures. The Bill before us today is only an offshot of the July 1983 recommendations. The first question, of course, is whether it faithfully reflects the public reaction. The 1983 Bill contained provisions which fell under three categories. First, it made it a criminal offence for anyone to own more than 20 per cent of the daily newspaper national circulation. This provision was to be administered by the Director of Investigation and Research appointed under the Combines Investigation Act.
Second, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission was empowered to assess the editorial impartiality of newspapers taken over by non-media corporations.
Third, an advisory council would have been established to hear public complaints wherever such a council would not already have been created by the provinces. I see that Bill C-226 does not contain the 1983 legislative provision concerning a press council. Other than that, there is not much difference between the two Bills. We must ask ourselves whether this Bill is a good policy for Canada with respect to newspapers. The Bill we are considering flows from the assumption that the existing legislation cannot solve the problems of the newspaper industry. We have to know whether that assumption is still valid. In other words, is the newspaper industry so different from other industries that it has to be regulated by a special act? If it is, will Bill C-226 solve the problems of that industry?
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comparison with the situation before 1975. Before then, most service industries were not covered by the general act pertaining to competition in Canada, namely the Combines Investigation Act. Many distinguished Members of the House will recall
that the Economic Council of Canada had raised a furore when it recommended that the service sector be governed by the Combines Investigation Act. The counter argument at the time was that service industries were different from manufacturing and resource industries.
And yet, service industries were responsible for a growing share of our national product. Fears were expressed that a wide-ranging legislation such as the Combines Investigation Act was not quite applicable to service industries. Indeed what a disgrace it would be to place the professions on the same footing as the manufacturing and the selling of products! It was pointed out that it was impossible to assess the quality or the quantity of the services provided. Many other objections were also put forward.
One of the major conclusions contained in the report of the Economic Council of Canada was that the competition policy should from now on apply to services. It said the following:
There is, in our view, enough evidence pointing to the existence in the service sector of the anti-competitive practices detrimental to the public interest to lead to the conclusion that the continued exemption of parts of this sector from competition policy cannot be justified. We therefore recommend, first, that the per se provisions of the revised Combines Investigation Act be made applicable to all commercial activities, including services provided in connection with the sale or rental of land and buildings and the unregulated activities of "regulated industries". The only major exemptions would be those which already exist in respect of bona fide trade union activities, and arrangements between fishermen in British Columbia and their customers. Some de facto exemptions would of course also continue in respect of activities clearly subject to alternate social control in the form of direct regulation or public ownership.
One of the effects of the recommended change would be to bring services related to "articles" immediately and clearly within the scope of the Act, without the protracted and socially wasteful litigation which the wording of the present legislation makes necessary in such cases. Personal services, such as those of hairdressers and travel agencies, would also be included, as would such business services as those provided by advertising agencies, building cleaners and telephone answering firms. The professions, financial institutions, a broad range of communications services, and all recreational services, including professional sports, would also be covered in so far as other types of social control did not apply.
The Council has observed a difference between goods and service industries in the sense that the products of the latter are intangible, and this creates problems, especially for consumers. Often, they are unable to check, return or resell what they are buying. In addition, they may have to purchase the service based only on an approximate assessment of the final costs. Such factors increase the need for competitive markets.
Another difference noted by the Council was the absence of import competition in many service industries. Actually, the nontransferability of some services also reduces internal competition.
While some people are asking that the law also apply to services, the Council had to examine whether some intrinsic aspect of true service industries justify their exemption simply because they provide services. After examining the question, the Council came to the conclusion that:

April 17, 1984

-while there are important differences in the nature of the products supplied by goods and service industries respectively, these differences are not such as to render an efficiency-oriented competition policy less relevant for service industries. On the contrary, it may in some ways be more relevant.
In 1975, the Combines Investigation Act was amended to apply to services generally. This is the policy of this Government with respect to competitive practices. This Government believes that the Combines Investigation Act should be universally applied.
As many are aware, in a few well-known cases, proceedings were undertaken against newspapers under the Combines Investigation Act. I refer mainly to the K.C. Irving case and more recently the Southam/Thomson case. Both these cases resulted in acquittals. Does this mean that a general legislation such as the Combines Investigation Act cannot be applied effectively to the newspaper industry? I do not know the answer to that. However, I doubt that such a conclusion could be drawn so quickly. Anyway, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) introduced a bill earlier this month to strengthen the Combines Investigation Act and make it more efficient. As many other members, I heard Mr. Fleming's comments on the legislation. Clearly, the Hon. Member for York-West feels that the Competition Bill cannot replace his own bill. In my view, the legislation put forward by the Hon. Judy Erola in many ways would deal much more efficiently with the newspaper industry than Bill C-226.
For instance, under Bill C-226, nobody could hold more than 20 per cent of the national, total circulation of daily newspapers. That provision is aimed at containing large newspaper chains. But competitionwise, would it not be better that there be a little more competition in New Brunswick for instance, where Irving controls 100 per cent of the market? An arbitrary figure bearing no relation to the relevant market would prevent the Southam or Thomson chains for instance from penetrating the New Brunswick market and perhaps compete efficiently with Irving. Moreover, there is nothing in Mr. Fleming's bill that would help remedy the situation in New Brunswick by making impossible for Irving to control 100 per cent of the provincial market.
On the other hand, the legislation put forward by the Hon. Judy Erola would require that large chains give notice to the Director of Investigation before going ahead with a merger. The merger would then be examined as to the degree of competition in the relevant market. Civil courts could issue orders to remedy the situation. That procedure in my view is more flexible and better adapted to the adjudication of newspaper mergers or takeovers than a bill based on arbitrary criteria leading to fines under criminal proceedings.
Under Bill C-226, the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission would make inquiries to assess the editorial independence of newspapers acquired by non-media corporations. Mr. Speaker, why should the Restrictive Trade Practices Commis-
Daily Newspaper Act
sion be asked to get involved in such matters? In giving the Commission powers of inquiry, is there no risk of jeopardizing the constitutional validity of the Combines Investigations Act?
It is not my contention that an amended Competition Act will solve all the problems in the newspaper industry. Far from that. I submit however that we should rely as far as possible on general laws, such as the Combines Investigations Act, to regulate the newspaper industry.
In my view, Parliament should discuss first the amendments to the Combines Investigations Act as proposed by the Hon. Judy Erola. In the course of that discussion, the parties concerned could be invited to put forward their views to a Standing Committee. The extension of the Combines Investigation Act to the newspaper industry could be one subject the Committee could study in depth.
As indicated by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Government is open to proposals for amending the Competition Bill, inasmuch as such proposals do not fly in the face of the aims of the bill. Although I commend the Hon. Member for York-West for his consistent efforts, I feel the House should look at other priorities. The special problems of the newspaper industry should be discussed at the relevant Standing Committee, during its discussion of Bill C-29, an Act to amend the Combines Investigation Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Burghardt (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: DAILY NEWSPAPER ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to join in the debate on Bill C-226, the Daily Newspaper Act, proposed by my hon. colleague from York West (Mr. Fleming). As he has already stated, this particular Bill in essence was originally proposed by the present Government as a document to, some suggest, stimulate discussion, and not necessarily as a hard and fast policy position. However, be that as it may, the Bill itself was never brought forth and introduced in Parliament. A great deal of discussion and comment has resulted. Hopefully, the present Government has taken the comments, views and wishes of those who have made representations regarding the original Daily Newspaper Act into consideration. That is perhaps the reason the legislation is not being presented by the Government.
In addressing Bill C-226, I would like to recall the circumstances which led the Government to propose the original Daily Newspaper Act. You may recall in 1980, and I believe the Hon. Member for York West has alluded to this fact, that the Southam and Thomson chains closed newspapers in Ottawa and Winnipeg. Although the director of investigation and research began an inquiry into this affair, the Government appointed Mr. Tom Kent to study the matter in the form of a royal commission. The royal commission on newspapers carefully studied the state of affairs in the newspaper industry and submitted a report which expressed concern on the high degree of market and ownership concentration in that industry as well as the need for measures to promote accountability and improve editorial quality of newspapers.

April 17, 1984
Daily Newspaper Act
When the Government put forward the proposed Daily Newspaper Act, it was with the full intention, I am sure, of soliciting views of members of the industry and the general public. The proposer of this Bill, the Hon. Member for York West, has mentioned the fact that much was said on the part of daily newspaper publishers and editorial writers regarding this particular Bill. I would suggest to the House, Mr. Speaker, that while much of this comment at the time perhaps seemed rather harsh and extremely critical of that particular Act, many of those comments have been taken into account. That is one of the reasons this legislation was never introduced in Parliament.
I think it is important to consider how the environment has changed since the events of 1980. I would like to take the opportunity to make a few observations on these changes which have taken place since the Government proposed the original Daily Newspaper Act. I would like to share some of my views on how these changes are likely to affect the newspaper industry today and, more important, in the future.
You may recall that on April 2 the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mrs. Erola) tabled proposals to amend the Combines Investigation Act. You may also recall that when the proposed Daily Newspaper Act was released a period of contentious debate followed. The criticisms that were levelled at that time included a statement that specific legislation geared toward a particular industry was a less preferred policy than the application of a general law of general application such as the Combines Investigation Act. The critics, however, conceded that the existing Combines Investigation Act needed to be strengthened. Indeed that is what the Minister's proposals are designed to do. The Combines Investigation Act, being a general law of general application, applies to all industries including newspapers. At the time the debate was going on I personally heard from a number of newspaper publishers and editors. They said that if the Combines Investigation Act of that time were strengthened it would look after some of the fears and concerns expressed by the Government and particularly the Cabinet of the day.
The proposals the Minister has put forward should alleviate these concerns about unchecked increases in concentration in Canadian markets. This, of course, applies to newspapers as well as it does to shoes. In the context of newspapers, I think I can safely venture that had the proposed Combines Investigation Act been in place in 1970, we would today have more competition and perhaps a lower degree of concentration in the newspaper industry. The Cities of Montreal, Ottawa, Winnipeg and Vancouver would have had a chance at having more than one resident English daily newspaper.
This is because the proposed amendments to the Combines Investigation Act make it a more flexible and pragmatic law which takes into account the business realities confronting Canadian firms. Mergers and joint production facilities in interests of efficiency gains would be allowed under the proposed Act. More significantly, and I think this is very important, the amendments would not treat businessmen as criminals. Rather, they would remedy the lessening of competition by taking all relevant market factors into account.
Another development I want to mention is the growth of voluntary press councils. The Hon. Member for York West has mentioned this because it was part of the original Daily Newspaper Act. He has dropped it from this particular Bill. I presume the reason is, of course, that initiatives have been taken by the newspaper industry itself to form voluntary press councils, to the extent that we now have councils in almost every province and region of the country from coast to coast.
Whether it can be argued that newspaper were forced into joining the voluntary press councils is another matter. There is no question that they certainly received the message and took the personal initiatives themselves and are now part of these voluntary press councils at which Canadians who have complaints or concerns to air about a particular newspaper can put their case forward. Hopefully their concerns will be dealt with in a very judicious, fair and equitable manner.
Finally, we know that the Kent Commission raised the issue of cross media ownership. It was in July of 1982 that the Governor in Council issued a directive to the CRTC pertaining to cross media ownership. We know that the directive asked the CRTC to examine, on a case by case basis, applications for broadcasting licenses by firms which also had a controlling interest in newspapers. This directive was partly designed to safeguard the independence in sources of news and information a community may receive. In issuing the directive, the Cabinet ensured that the CRTC would continue to have flexibility and discretion over matters that it is best equipped to deal with.
It is my understanding that to date, the CRTC has applied the directive in seven cases. However, I must admit that there is one aspect of the directive on cross media ownership that troubles me. As an example, let me cite a case in my own area of London, Ontario, where a particular company owns the only daily newspaper plus an AM radio station, an FM radio station and a television station. In applying for a renewal of the licence for its AM radio station, it had to address the issue of the cross media ownership, and rightly so because this was the Cabinet directive handed to the CRTC.
This particular company was prepared to address this particular issue to try to prove to the CRTC that especially in the area of news and information services, the individual companies did operate independently of each other. The CRTC eventually renewed the AM radio station licence and in doing so issued a glowing report about this particular company's independent operations when it came to news and public service events as it pertained to the four media outlets.
Approximately two months following the issuance of that AM radio licence, the same company had to apply for renewal of its FM radio licence. In my view it is unfortunate that it had to address again the issue of cross media ownership. This took a lot of time, money and effort on the part of the company. It had already been given a clean bill of health when it received its AM radio licence. It had to go through the whole procedure
April 17, 1984

again in receiving renewal of the FM licence. Probably in another two months' time when it applies for renewal of the television licence, it will have to do the same thing again.
I would respectfully suggest that this is one area of Cabinet directive on cross media ownership that should be changed. Perhaps the Cabinet would take this into consideration, still allowing the CRTC to address the areas of concern and need. But once they have arrived at a particular decision, I feel that a company should not have to go through the same process time and time again.
I would like to reiterate that there have been significant changes in the general environment as it pertains to the newspaper industry. However, this is not to say that concerns in this area do not remain. I congratulate the Hon. Member for York West for bringing this Bill to the floor of the House of Commons at this time. But the solutions we may seek need to be tempered somewhat by the changes that I have mentioned.
I suggest that the House should give quick passage to Bill C-29 which looks after the entire area of competitiveness and combines investigation and the like so as to modernize the competition laws of Canada. This will give us an opportunity to stimulate newspaper competition. After we see how well the competition laws deal with the issue, perhaps we will be in a better position to see whether we do in fact need Bill C-226.

subtopic: DAILY NEWSPAPER ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the previous speaker mentioned, the Bill before us today would place limits on the concentration of ownership of daily newspapers in Canada at the national level. Presumably its purpose is to ensure that concentration does not lead to restrictions on the freedom of the press or reduce diversity of opinion. It is assumed therefore, that concentration of ownership restricts freedom of the press and that concentration somehow restricts diversity of opinion. That is the assumption upon which this Bill was written.
The problem is that there really is no conclusive proof that concentration of ownership has such a result. I would like to point out to the House that it may be that concentration of ownership, in certain circumstances, may encourage a diversity of opinion.
The evidence is as follows. First, as many observers of newspapers can readily conclude, there has been a great increase in the number of one newspaper cities in the United States, Canada and Europe. One would assume that this would decrease the diversity of opinion. What has happened, however, is that there is a great diversity of news available through a variety of newspapers, all owned by the same person or company in many instances. There is competition within a newspaper. We are all aware of the journalists who often take opposing views on the same subjects and we find their views on the same day, on the same page of many newspapers in North America.
There is also competition within the media. Traditional types of newspapers, which I believe are referred to as broad sheet papers-I stand to be corrected-have been replaced in

subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS BY 1NCO AT PORT COLBORNE. (B) JOB RETRAINING INQUIRY
LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS BY 1NCO AT PORT COLBORNE. (B) JOB RETRAINING INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a result of questions I raised a short while ago, I would like to deal with the subject of research and development, a topic which has seen some media coverage in the last few weeks from Liberal leadership contenders who are filling the air with rhetoric on that subject and, indeed, on other subjects as well. Sometimes it is difficult to distinguish between what is Liberal Party policy and what is being said by these mini-Prime Ministers for their own purposes.
Perhaps we will have to wait until the leadership convention is over before the current Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) will once again have to contend with reality instead of catering to the whims of delegates to the June convention. It is easy to say that he will sell PetroCan stations and make many other promises when he has aspirations to be Prime Minister. However, if the Minister really wanted to be Prime Minister he should have taken part in last year's convention.
There is a lack of adequate incentives for companies to indulge in adequate research and development. Hand in hand with that is the lack of facilities for retraining workers who face extinction due to the ever-changing needs of the high-tech workplace. A case in point is the closing of a manufacturing plant in Fort Erie called Hart & Cooley, throwing about 70 people out of work. I think the first priority of those charged with the development of science and technology should be to get rid of the "pie in the sky" attitude which deals in science fiction rhetoric and concocts wonderful generalities about happenings in the future. What we need is a common sense approach to the questions facing taxpayers and indeed voters, not only in the 1990s but right now.
Take, for example, the response given by the Minister to a question directed to him by the Conservative spokesman on science and technology, the Hon. Member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon). The Hon. Member requested that the Government make a co-ordinated effort to ensure that jobs connected to the space program come to Canada. He specifically asked that the 88 Canadian companies that have already submitted proposals for contracts with the space program be given first consideration in the awarding of any contracts.
Instead of answering this specific question, the Minister carried on with generalities which gave no indication that he was prepared to guarantee that Canadians get priority in the letting of contracts. This is indicative of the Minister's and,
indeed, of the Government's very fuzzy approach to the whole question of science and technology. It is clearly this approach that has led to the current lack of opportunities for Canadians in this very important field.
This attitude was underlined again in the last Budget which was supposed to consolidate the recovery, yet failed to extend research and development benefits as defined under the Income Tax Act to the development of computer software. This is one area which will bring Canada to the forefront of the high technology world, yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) failed to give consideration to helping out that fledgling industry, nor did he even consider adding to the funding available for the total research and development package sufficient funding to bring it back to the level which it enjoyed back in the year 1968.
Let us have some assistance for what I feel is a very important program. Otherwise we may find ourselves at the portal of the year 2000 with the technology of the 1970s, and we will have to blame someone for this problem. No doubt the Minister of Finance will be chosen for that honour along with the Minister of State for Science and Technology. To avoid such a scenario, it is absolutely essential that modern industry develop new products to make use of the workers and processes made obsolete.
Let me take a case in point. The Inco plant in Port Colborne had to lay off 490 workers because of decreased demand for its electrolytic nickel. Why does this kind of thing need to occur? It is a disaster, Mr. Speaker, when in a town of 20,000 people, 500 people are laid off. I know that is not the mandate of Government to tell private industry if it can or cannot shut down a plant or lay off workers. This is approaching too much the ideals of our friends to the left, physically as well as philosophically. However, it does make sense to provide adequate financial incentives to such companies to look into new markets and innovative products. That is what we need to do.
The same people in the same place could be manufacturing the products of the 1980s instead of opting for the nice sounding but unpleasant prospect of early retirement. One group which must not be forgotten is the unemployed people who are over 40 years of age, many of whom will have great difficulty indeed being rehired because of their age and lack of up-to-date skills. Therefore, the Government must take the responsibility to ensure that these people are retrained and encouraged to once again enter the work force. The Government must help them out of the lonely abyss in which they find themselves when they are too young to retire and too old to be easily redirected to another career.
Who is to blame for this problem? Indeed, the Government must accept some of the blame for not encouraging companies to pursue the new markets they need and the development of new products. The companies too must take some of the blame for not devoting more of their energies to those directions.
In conclusion, it seems sad and incomprehensible that we in Canada are spending only a shade over 1 per cent of our GNP on research and development while our competitors are spending considerably more. With a GNP like that of the United
April 17, 1984

States, the amount of money spent is staggering, and it appears certain that if the same trend continues we are doomed to have a second rate branch plant economy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
subtopic: LABOUR CONDITIONS-LAY-OFFS BY 1NCO AT PORT COLBORNE. (B) JOB RETRAINING INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy that the Hon. Member arrived at the point of the question. When he began to speak, I was surprised; I thought he was dealing with the wrong subject when asking his question. The question is with regard to Inco at Port Colborne. I have a reply for him concerning the question he asked on April 3. I hope that the point 1 make tonight answers the question he asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts), not the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston). I am not sure he was really on the point of the question. I have a response regarding the Inco situation which I will give in French.
[Translation\
As the Hon. Member for Erie (Mr. Fretz) is certainly aware, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian mining industry has been dealt a severe blow these past few years because of the softening of the demand on the international market. That is one of the reasons why INCO has decided to end its production of electrolytic nickel in Port Colborne. This restraint measure should improve INCO's position as a low cost nickel producer. The resulting layoffs will affect 415 hourly-paid workers who have received a 12 week advance notice, except those with over five years of service who are entitled to a severance pay of one week salary for each year of service up to a maximum of 26 weeks. In order to minimize the actual number of layoffs, the company has offered to study, together with representatives of Section 6200 of the United Steelworkers of America, programs of early retirement for eligible hourly-paid workers. They hope that by encouraging eligible workers to opt for an early retirement, they can reduce the actual number of layoffs. Some 75 other salaried employees will be laid off. The company has hired an independent professional counselling firm to help salaried employees thus affected to secure other jobs, to move to other areas or to plan their retirement. INCO has offered to examine manpower adjustment issues with Canada Employment and Immigration Commission officials and union representatives, and to set up a committee of the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council for the purpose of suggesting ways of helping these workers by offering them new jobs and career retraining. CEIC officials for the Ontario region have contacted INCO's representatives who have confirmed their intention to set up a committee of the Canada Employment and Immigration Advisory Council. CEIC officials are to meet with union representatives to seek their support for this committee. The CEIC will study the economic context of the Port Colborne community and surrounding area to determine whether these special manpower adjustment measures are warranted. In the past,
Adjournment Debate
such cooperation between the CEIC, INCO and the union have solved similar problems resulting from job losses. I believe their continued cooperation will alleviate the current situation.

That is the reply I have for the Member concerning the question he asked of the Minister of Employment and Immigration on April 3.

subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-USE OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS TO INCREASE REPRESENTATION. (B) CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION VACANCY
VISIBLE MINORITIES-USE OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS TO INCREASE REPRESENTATION. (B) CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION VACANCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will address my question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Gourd). I am pleased he is here this evening. It follows a question I raised yesterday regarding the use of Governor in Council appointments to increase the participation of visible minorities on boards and commissions. I am, of course, following up on some of the recommendations in the Equality Now report. I begin by quoting one of the black actresses who said;
If we are not accurately seen in the mirror that the media holds up to society, then clearly we are somehow not part of that society.
This last weekend at a conference in Winnipeg, which I referred to in my question, there was Focus on the Visible Minorities in Advertising Conference. We heard a very touching story from Ron Nadeau with native communications. He gave the illustration of a young native boy in school whose teacher asked him to cut out of the catalogue a picture of somebody who looked like his family.
The young native boy wrote to one of the catalogue companies and said: "I was not able to fulfil the request of my teacher because when I looked in your catalogue there was nobody like my family. Everybody was white." He said to the catalogue company: "In the next catalogue, I hope you will have somebody who looks like me."
There are seven Indian reserves in my constituency. The Indian chiefs often ask me why there are never any Indians in the advertising that we see over television. That same conference dealt with the question of the participation of visible minorities in advertising. I was a bit disturbed and appalled. Ad agencies and even large companies with public relations departments that spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on advertising failed to be present at that conference.
We should focus on the CRTC and various boards that deal with regulations and the way that visible minorities are portrayed in Canada because they have an awful lot of legislative clout. In terms of the impact on Canadian citizens the CRTC, and possibly the CTC, the Canadian Transport Commission, have an enormous amount of weight, and both have a fantastic impact on Canadian citizens.
Recommendation 21 of Equality Now report of a committee on which I had the privilege to serve, urges the federal Government to use Governor in Council appointments, to

April 17, 1984
Adjournment Debate
increase the participation of visible minorities on federal boards and commissions. On page 51 of that report we specifically refer to the CRTC.
When I asked the Minister yesterday to act on this matter, I specifically referred to the CRTC. He said he was very happy with the general principle of the participation of all racial and of all other groups of our society on these boards. But the 19-member board of the CRTC is an all-white board. There are no participants of the visible minorities. I was urging the Government to consider the fact that presently there is a vacancy. In fact, that vacancy has been there since February of 1983, for over one year. There is an opportunity for the Government to make sure there is a chance for all members of our society to participate.
There is a myth out there that all the visible minorities are not qualified. There have been enough studies which have shown that that is not true. In fact, the CBC had a trainee program and instead of using the old boys' network to advertise for the applications, they used the ethnic press and ethnic media. There were 800 applications of which they themselves judged at least 150 were eminently qualified to fill the eight positions which existed.
We are not asking for quotas. None of the visible minorities have ever asked for quotas. We are not asking that unqualified people be appointed. We are saying there are qualified people. Let us get going and implement some of the recommendations of Equality Now. Let us have some action now. I hope that the Minister will, if he has not done any kind of survey or study, undertake to make sure that in our society there is an equitable participation of all members of society, of all ethnic cultural groups, especially after the Equality Now report of the visible minorities in our society. I will await the answer of the Parliamentary Secretary. I hope that it is a much better one than the answer I received from the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Collenette) yesterday.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Gourd (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
subtopic: VISIBLE MINORITIES-USE OF GOVERNOR IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS TO INCREASE REPRESENTATION. (B) CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION VACANCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as usual, the Hon. Member gets all his ideas mixed up. He talks about appointments, about the CRTC, about the CBC. All this is just a pretext to deliver a speech in front of his constituents. As for the answer to his question-

*-it is the practice of the federal Government to use Governor in Council appointments to increase the participation of visible minorities on federal boards and commissions, as well as in the senior management of the Public Service and Crown corporations. The Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Collenette) since assuming office has been increasingly active in the promotion of candidates to various boards and commissions as positions became vacant.
The Minister recognized that the federal Government must tap the immense pool of talent and experience which is present in the visible minority community.

I could easily quote a number of people from visible minorities who have been appointed to various functions within commissions or the federal Public Service: Mrs. Ann Cools who was elevated to the Senate; Jean Augustine, who was appointed to the Royal Commission on the Status of Women; Juanita Westmorland-Traore, to the Canadian Human Rights Commission; Jean Gamage, to the Harbourfront Corporation; Tom Shoyama, to Petro-Canada and to the Royal Commission on the Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada; and Mr. David Suzuki, to the Science Council of Canada.
In addition, the Minister of State for Multiculturalism has brought the matter of Governor in Council appointments of visible minorities to the attention of his Cabinet colleagues. He is confident they will all recognize the importance of that community and its contribution to this country.

I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this provides an adequate answer to my hon. colleague.

subtopic: FISHERIES-COWICHAN ESTUARY-GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) APPLICATION OF POLICY
FISHERIES-COWICHAN ESTUARY-GOVERNMENT POLICY. (B) APPLICATION OF POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since 1980 when this Parliament began I have been concerned and on a number of occasions have raised the issue of the Cowichan estuary. The people who live in that area, fishermen on the British Columbia coast, and myself as their representative, have been trying to get the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to protect the estuary as a very important part of our fish habitat. The importance of estuaries in the life cycle of salmon has only been recently recognized, but it is becoming increasingly clear that unless we protect our estuaries we do not have any hope of maintaining a salmon industry on the Pacific coast.
The destruction of fish habitat, Mr. Speaker, is equivalent to the destruction of the fishing industry. That in fact is what we see happening in British Columbia today. The neglect of fish habitat by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans is a very important piece in the jugsaw puzzle of fisheries mismanagement. As they say, the chickens are now coming home to roost, but unfortunately the salmon are not coming home to spawn.
We face a very serious crisis on the Pacific coast. Cutbacks on fishing time for trawlers to supposedly help conserve dwindling stocks of Chinook salmon mean these fishermen are not going to be able to get enough weeks in fishing to qualify for their UIC benefits. They are cut back to two months instead of
April 17, 1984

the usual five and a half months. That is one indication of the Department's mismanagement of that situation. As the President of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union said, the fisheries policy is really a fast track to bankruptcy for these trollers. The restrictions on the Gulf trolling fleet will be followed soon by restrictions on other gear types.
The Cowichan estuary is critical to one of the most important Chinook stocks off Vancouver Island. The loss of habitat there is inexcusable and will result in the direct loss of jobs. As a result of a trade-off or sell-out that the Minister participated in, Doman's Mill was able to trade 23 acres of farmland for the right to boom logs in some 40 acres of inter-tidal area within the estuary. Then the Minister and his Department have the nerve to call this a no-net loss of fish habitat. Let us get this straight, Mr. Speaker. We are not questioning Doman's right to be on the estuary and have some booming grounds. That was recognized several years ago. But we do question the need to expand that booming ground. The local economy badly needs the jobs at Doman's Mill, but it also needs the jobs in the tourist and fishing industry which will be lost if we do not protect our estuary. The mill does not need extra booming area.
A 1978 study for the fisheries and marine service of the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, which was Appendix 11 of the Cowichan Estuary Task Force Report, estimated that at times Doman's were storing logs in the estuary in excess of 14 months. This is far beyond the normal requirements for a mill storing logs. It recommended that there should be a 20 acre limit for Doman's to store logs in the estuary. I would like to hear from the Department and the Minister why the Fisheries department abandoned that policy. Why did they abandon the policy of saying there would be a 20 acre limit for Doman industry to boom in that area.
On December 20 I asked the Minister questions about the so-called no-net loss policy. I asked if there would be a public process for any exchanges that were made. The Minister assured me that that would in fact happen. However, it did not happen. In fact, the public was kept completely in the dark about the conditions of the exchange. Members of the Cowichan Estuary Preservation Society were in fact isolated from everything that was happening. Fisheries Department officials did not even answer their phone calls.
I am not a person who traditionally likes to engage in bashing bureaucrats. I think that generally speaking they do a good job. However, there seemed to be some directive from on high that prevented these people from dealing in an open way with the people from the Cowichan Estuary Preservation Society. We want to know what studies were done to determine if the exchange was in fact a fair exchange, and if in fact there was a no-net loss of habitat. If there were any studies I urge the Minister to release them and make them available. I suspect that we will be waiting a long time because I do not think any study can possibly justify the trading of 23 acres of farmland for 40 acres of very valuable intertidal estuary area.
Adjournment Debate
We want answers. The public is entitled to answers on this very important public resource. We want to know why there is a sell-out of our fisheries and a betrayal of fish habitat. We want to know if that is the pattern that will be followed with the Kemano II project. I would very much appreciate if the Parliamentary Secretary could be straightforward in the answers he gives to these questions.

Mr. Speaker, representing the beautiful constituency of Restigouche in the Atlantic area where we have the Atlantic salmon coming up the rivers to spawn, newsprint mills and the importance of forestry and fishing, I can fully understand the concern that is being brought forward here this afternoon by the Hon. Member. However, I would hasten to remind the Hon. Member that he would have had an equal opportunity to pose his questions at the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry the other day when we devoted the entire time to questions relating to the Pacific Coast. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, we had officials on hand at the Standing Committee to respond directly on fishery matters in greater detail than we would have had the time for in the House.
However, the Hon. Member has raised a number of questions relating to the Cowichan Estuary and our Department's fish habitat management policy. In recent times the Minister himself and other Department officials have been making statements with respect to fish management, salmon management and the whole range of the subject he has raised here today.
The waters of the Cowichan estuary on Vancouver Island have been used for storing logs by a number of forest companies for many years. Our Department has been negotiating with these companies and with the Province of British Columbia to reduce the total amount of log storage in fish habitat areas within the estuary. I am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to announce that our regional staff are finalizing arrangements with these companies and the B.C. Government which will result in a reduction of more than 50 per cent of the total acreage of log storage in the estuary. This reduction will result in the restoration of valuable fish habitat and serves to illustrate well the fish habitat restoration goal which is clearly outlined in our Department's discussion paper Toward a Fish Habitat Management Policy.
Not only will fish habitat currently altered by log storage be restored but, in addition, some land in the estuary, which is currently not available as fish habitat, will be developed into productive fish habitat as part of our overall habitat improvement efforts in the estuary. This will serve to further increase the total amount of productive fish habitat in the estuary. The Cowichan estuary is thus an excellent example of the kind of habitat restoration project our department will be pursuing through the implementation of the fish habitat management policy.
